oneLiner.en: At a bris around Purim, the Rav explains that milah, done on a child without understanding, expresses the hidden point of Avraham Avinu in every Jew that is above intellect, the same point revealed on Purim 'until one does not know'.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the verse that the Jews had light, gladness, joy and honor, and the Gemara's reading that joy is milah and honor is tefillin. Purim, he says, reveals the hidden root in every Jew: a Jew has free choice, but he also has a pintele Yid, a point from the Avos that cannot be extinguished, which Hashem guards as 'Magen Avraham'. This point is above intellect, which is why even simple Jews give their lives for emunah, and why on Purim Jews reach 'until one does not know'. Milah is the bris of Avraham Avinu, the first Jew, and so it is done on a child who has no understanding: its depth is above daas. Tefillin, in contrast, is a mitzvah of daas. Together they make up a Yiddishkeit both above and within understanding. He closes with blessings for the child and the family.

en: Every Jew has free choice, but he also carries a pintele Yid from the Avos that can never be extinguished.
This point of Avraham Avinu is above intellect, which is why even simple Jews give their lives for emunah.
Purim, when Jews reach 'until one does not know', reveals this point that is above daas.
Milah is done on a child without understanding because, as the bris of Avraham Avinu, it is above daas.
Tefillin, unlike milah, is a mitzvah bound up with daas.

title.en: Purim and the unquenchable point of Avraham

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that 'sasson' is milah and 'yikar' is tefillin, and explains that Purim reveals the hidden point of Avraham Avinu in every Jew, a pintele Yid above intellect that Hashem guards as 'Magen Avraham' and that shows itself in mesirus nefesh and in 'until one does not know'.

title.en: Milah above daas, tefillin with daas

summary.en: The Rav asks why the great mitzvah of milah is done on an infant without understanding, and answers that as the bris of Avraham Avinu it is above daas, unlike tefillin, which is a mitzvah of daas. He closes with blessings for the child and the family.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - Shushan Purim

oneLiner.en: At a bris seudah on Shushan Purim, the Rav explains that Megillas Esther and Purim hold only a glimmer of the light of Moshiach, since the wiping out of Amalek is not yet complete, and that a bris milah, like Purim, removes the orlah and reveals that light.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara: Esther asked the Chachamim to write her book for all generations, and they answered that Amalek may be written only three times, not four. He asks why, and adds Shmuel's view that Esther is not one of the holy writings, though the twenty-four books are the ornaments of the Shechinah. He explains that every book existed in heaven before its navi wrote it; Megillas Esther holds a spark of the light of Moshiach, given to accustom the eyes, and Purim is not yet complete because Amalek is not yet wiped out. Bringing the Bnei Yissaschar and the Chasam Sofer, he links Purim to bris milah: both remove the orlah and reveal a glimpse of Moshiach. He applies this to the bris seudah on Shushan Purim, blesses the child and family, and closes by answering his opening question.

en: The Chachamim hesitated to write Megillas Esther because the Torah allows Amalek's war to be written three times, and a fourth time would require a complete wiping out of Amalek.
The twenty-four books of Tanach are the ornaments of the Shechinah, and each book existed in heaven before its navi drew it down into writing.
Megillas Esther and Purim hold a spark of the light of Moshiach, given so that Jews can grow used to that light before it comes in full.
Purim is not yet a finished yom tov, since its essence is the wiping out of Amalek, which is not yet complete.
A bris milah, like Purim, removes the orlah and reveals a glimpse of the days of Moshiach, so the Shushan Purim seudah is a seudah of bris milah.

title.en: Why Amalek may be written only three times

summary.en: The Rav opens with Esther's request to be written for all generations and the Chachamim's answer that Amalek may be written only three times, and asks why. He adds Shmuel's view that Esther is not one of the holy writings, and asks how that fits with the twenty-four books corresponding to the twenty-four combinations of the Name Adnus.

title.en: The Megillah holds the light of Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav explains that every navi's book existed in heaven before he wrote it, and that Megillas Esther holds a spark of the light of Moshiach, given to accustom Jews to that light. Since Purim's essence is the wiping out of Amalek, which is not yet complete, the Megillah's place among the holy writings is still hidden in heaven until Moshiach comes.

title.en: Purim, bris milah and the removal of the orlah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the Megillah has the laws of the holy writings only on Purim, and explains that on Purim Jews receive a glimpse of the days of Moshiach. He shows that a bris milah gives the same glimpse, brings the Chasam Sofer that 'Megillah' stands for removing idolatry from the land, and concludes that a Shushan Purim seudah is a seudah of bris milah.

title.en: A bris seudah on Shushan Purim

summary.en: The Rav says this bris seudah differs from others: on Shushan Purim every Jew who keeps Purim properly receives a measure of bris milah, is freed from his evil part, and can make a new covenant with Hashem. He praises the child's family of Torah, Chassidus and yiras Shamayim and blesses the child and the family to see the light of Moshiach.

title.en: Why the Chachamim finally wrote the Megillah

summary.en: After finishing his blessings, the Rav returns to his opening question: Yehoshua, Shaul, and Mordechai and Esther each only weakened Amalek, and the Megillah, written in concealment without Hashem's name, shows the wiping out is not yet complete. The Chachamim wrote it once they understood that Hashem wanted Haman's descendants to learn Torah in Bnei Brak, and they were content with the glimpse of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: לבינוני אין לו כח לעקור הרע לגמרי אבל יכול י"ד לשלוט עליו בפועל ממש. ביאור איך העבירה הוא שטות. לבינוני יש תאוות לדברים גשמיים אבל מצד שורשו בקדושה הוא מואס ברע.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the beinoni's mind can rule over his yetzer hara in deed but cannot uproot it, except in times of revealed love between Hashem and the Jew, such as davening and the month of Adar.

abstract.en: The Rav continues the Tanya on the beinoni: he never sins, but the evil in the left chamber of the heart remains at full strength, and only Hashem's help lets him overcome it. This answers the Tanya's question from the first chapter: he is called 'like a rasha' because he could fall. He warns that the yetzer grows stronger with age and indulgence, and that constant learning is no sign it is gone. The mind rules the heart in thought, speech and deed, yet cannot expel the yetzer, except in times of revealed love, as in davening. From here he speaks of Hashem's hidden love for every Jew: the Ruzhiner's story, the father and son, the sin of the Golden Calf, and Purim, where the salvation was prepared at Achashverosh's party. He explains hester panim, the struggle of Yaakov and Esav, Yerushalayim and Rome, and Adar Sheni.

en: The beinoni never sins, but the yetzer hara in the left chamber of the heart remains as strong as at birth; he wins only because Hashem stands at his right side and helps him.
He is called 'like a rasha' because the potential to sin is fully alive in him, so he must not believe people who call him a tzaddik.
The mind was created with power to rule the heart's urges in thought, speech and deed, but not to uproot the yetzer itself.
In times of favor, above all during davening, the love of Hashem is revealed and the beinoni is temporarily like a tzaddik.
Hashem's love for every Jew is the unconditional love of a father for a child, concealed but revealed in times of favor, even through the people's sins.
Adar is a time of hester panim within which Hashem's hidden love is uncovered, as the Megillah shows the salvation being prepared during the sin itself.

title.en: The beinoni and the three judges

summary.en: The Rav reviews the difference between the tzaddik, who has eliminated his yetzer hara, and the beinoni, whose yetzer remains at full strength in the left chamber of the heart. He explains that Hashem is the third judge who stands at the right of the 'pauper' and gives him the added strength to win.

title.en: Why the beinoni is 'like a rasha'

summary.en: The Rav shows how this answers the Tanya's question from the first chapter: why someone who never sins should see himself 'like a rasha'. Since the yetzer is fully present, he could fall, so he must not believe those who call him a tzaddik.

title.en: The yetzer grows stronger with age

summary.en: The Rav stresses the importance of the years of youth with the mashal of grapes and of a young sapling, and explains that indulgence makes a person coarser as he ages. Even constant learning for the sake of the mitzvah is no sign that the yetzer has left.

title.en: The mind rules the heart, but cannot uproot

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem created the mind with power over the heart, so the beinoni keeps his thought, speech and deed from serving the yetzer, and there is no excuse of 'I couldn't help it'. But the mind cannot expel the yetzer itself, except in special times when the love of Hashem is revealed.

title.en: Times of favor and the Ruzhiner's story

summary.en: The Rav explains that during davening, an eis ratzon, the beinoni is like a tzaddik, and mentions Rosh Chodesh Adar and Adar Sheni as such times. He tells how the Ruzhiner told a chassid that Hashem's love for a notorious sinner in the town far exceeds the Rebbe's love for his chassidim.

title.en: A father's love and the Golden Calf

summary.en: The Rav contrasts a master, who loves servants by their devotion, with a father, whose love for his child has no reason and no conditions. He explains why Moshe Rabbeinu stressed how great the sin of the Golden Calf was: like a child who broke a leg, the damage itself arouses the father's mercy.

title.en: Achashverosh's party and the hidden salvation

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Golden Calf brought out the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, culminating on Yom Kippur, and that Purim is like it. He brings the Gemara on Achashverosh's miscalculation of the seventy years and the Chasam Sofer's point that at the very party where the Jews sinned, Hashem was already preparing their salvation through Vashti's removal.

title.en: Hester panim and the month of Adar

summary.en: The Rav explains the double concealment of 'haster astir' with the Ba'al Shem Tov's mashal of a child who knows or does not know his father is near. Adar is a time of hester, and its task is to uncover in the Megillah Hashem's love; Adar and Nissan are months of favor.

title.en: The beinoni during davening

summary.en: The Rav explains that only the beinoni is freed from the yetzer during davening, while someone who often stumbles is disturbed by bad thoughts even in Shema. Even then, the beinoni's mind only controls the yetzer and does not uproot it.

title.en: Yaakov and Esav, Yerushalayim and Rome

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's verse about the constant struggle of Yaakov and Esav, where one rises as the other falls, in soul, place and time. Yerushalayim faces Rome, a kingdom of many nations, and he brings the Bluzhever Rebbe's teaching on Yerushalayim written with or without a yud.

title.en: Adar Sheni, outside the count

summary.en: The Rav says the subject needs more time to explain. He then explains that Adar Sheni, like Dan at the rear of the camp, stands outside the twelve combinations of Hashem's name, so its hester is stronger and its miracle greater. He adds that Esav, like the pig showing its split hooves, displays virtues he lacks.

title.en: On pronunciation and old customs

summary.en: In a partly garbled exchange the Rav speaks about pronunciation of loshon hakodesh: no community today has the exact original havara, yet Hashem accepts our speech like parents who understand a small child. He ends advising to stick to the established halachos and customs of Klal Yisroel and not take on new chumros that leave a person nervous.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in Nissan, the Rav links the removal of the orlah to the removal of chametz, which stands for the yetzer hara, and to the hope that Hashem will clear the world of evil.

abstract.en: Speaking at a bris held in the month of Nissan, the Rav opens with the Haggadah's words about the son who asks, and speaks of Eliyahu HaNavi, who comes to the bris, in connection with questions and with the season of freedom. He then turns to chametz: it has many names, but they all point to one thing, the yetzer hara, the leaven in the dough. Milah, he says, carries the theme of Aleinu, removing impurity from the land and perfecting the world under the kingship of Hashem. This bris is no ordinary one: it falls in Nissan, when Jews are busy with biur chametz. Just as we search out and clear away our chametz, the Rav asks that Hashem clear away the chametz and the yetzer hara from the whole world. He closes with brachos for the family and those honored at the bris, and for the zechus of Pesach and the korban Pesach.

en: Chametz has many names, but they all refer to one thing, the yetzer hara.
Milah carries the theme of Aleinu: removing impurity from the land and perfecting the world under Hashem's kingship.
A bris in Nissan, during biur chametz, calls for the prayer that Hashem clear the chametz and the yetzer hara from the world.

title.en: The son who asks and Eliyahu HaNavi

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Haggadah's words about the son who asks, and speaks of Eliyahu HaNavi in connection with questions and the time of freedom. Much of this stretch is too garbled to follow.

title.en: Chametz, the yetzer hara and milah

summary.en: The Rav explains that chametz stands for the yetzer hara and ties milah to Aleinu's hope of clearing impurity from the world. Since this bris falls during biur chametz, he asks that Hashem clear away the world's chametz, and closes with brachos for the family and for Pesach.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - RCH Nissan

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Rosh Chodesh Nissan, the Rav presents the bris as a foretaste of the days of Moshiach and sees this day, and this year's calendar, as a special opening for the Geulah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by describing a bris as a kind of preview of the revelation of Moshiach: the orlah is removed, recalling the hope of removing impurity from the land and perfecting the world under Hashem's kingship. He cites the Lubliner on the bris as a glimpse of the days of Moshiach, and notes that the Harachaman prayers at a bris mention Eliyahu HaNavi and Moshiach. He then turns to the day: Rosh Chodesh Nissan took ten crowns, among them being the first day of creation, and this year it fell on Sunday. He adds that a year in which Erev Pesach falls on Shabbos is described as a great sign for Moshiach's coming, so this simcha can help bring the Geulah awaited by all the worlds. He closes by praising the family, recalling an elder of the family, Reb Yechezkel, a great talmid chacham, and blessing the child.

en: A bris is a preview of the revelation of Moshiach, and the removal of the orlah recalls the hope of removing impurity from the world.
Rosh Chodesh Nissan took ten crowns, one being the first day of creation, and this year it fell on Sunday.
A year in which Erev Pesach falls on Shabbos is described as a great sign for the coming of Moshiach.
This simcha can help bring the Geulah that all the upper and lower worlds await.

summary.en: The Rav describes the bris as a preview of the revelation of Moshiach, ties the removal of the orlah to the hope of removing impurity from the world, cites the Lubliner, and notes that the Harachaman prayers at a bris mention Eliyahu and Moshiach.

title.en: Rosh Chodesh Nissan, its crowns and the Geulah

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the ten crowns of Rosh Chodesh Nissan, notes that this year it fell on Sunday and Erev Pesach on Shabbos, a sign for Moshiach, and says this simcha can help bring the Geulah. He then praises the family, recalls Reb Yechezkel, and blesses the child.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - Korban Nasi Dan

oneLiner.en: At a bris on the day of the korban of the Nasi of Dan, the Rav explains that Hashem takes pride in Dan, the last tribe, as in the last generation of galus, and that the child brought to the bris is a korban before the Shechinah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the day's reading of the korban of Achiezer ben Ammishaddai, the Nasi of the tribe of Dan, and the Midrash on Hashem's words 'this is the korban'. Dan was a lowly tribe, some of whose people were cast out and exposed to Amalek in war, yet Hashem made a special yom tov for each tribe, and today is the yom tov of Dan. Dan traveled last, gathering in all the camps, and the Rav sees in this the end of galus: we, at the end of the exile, are in the period of Dan, and Hashem rejoices and boasts of us before the angels. Chazal liken bringing a child to his bris to bringing a korban, so the child is offered before the Shechinah. The last generation, the heel before Moshiach, will be the greatest of all generations, greater even than the generation of Yetzias Mitzrayim. He closes by blessing the child to grow in Torah and good deeds, and the parents and grandparents with nachas.

en: Hashem made a special yom tov for each tribe through its Nasi's korban, and today is the yom tov of the tribe of Dan.
Dan, which traveled last and gathered in all the camps, corresponds to the end of galus, the time we are in.
Chazal liken bringing a child to his bris to bringing a korban, so the child is offered before the Shechinah.
The last generation, the heel before Moshiach, will be the greatest of all, greater than the generation of Yetzias Mitzrayim.

title.en: The korban of Dan and the last generation

summary.en: The Rav opens with the korban of Achiezer ben Ammishaddai, the Nasi of Dan: Dan was a lowly tribe and traveled last, like us at the end of galus, yet Hashem boasts of it, and the child at the bris is a korban before the Shechinah. The last generation, he says, will be the greatest, and he closes with brachos for the child and family.

catalogTitle: לבינוני אין לו הבחירה להיות צדיק ממש שמואס ברע באמת' אלא שונא רע מצד שכליות. עצות לכך.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Tanya chapter 14: the beinoni cannot make himself abhor evil like a tzaddik, but he can always control his deeds, speech and thoughts, and he can overcome his yetzer hara by awakening the hidden love of Hashem that would make him give his life rather than serve avodah zarah.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews the tzaddik, who has done away with his yetzer hara, and the rasha, and then turns to the beinoni of Tanya chapter 14, whose lifelong struggle is the calling of most people. The beinoni cannot choose what his heart desires, and a stronger urge may even come from being raised to a higher level, but he can always control what he does, says and thinks. Every aveira is like avodah zarah, and every Jew has a hidden love of Hashem that would make him give his life rather than worship an idol, as a story of a Jewish thief shows. Answering a question, the Rav explains that resisting daily is a real mesiras nefesh. The advice is to tell oneself: I do not want to be a rasha even for a moment. He connects the hidden love to the fortieth level of a person, Yom Kippur and the Rambam on forced consent, discusses lost bechirah, levels of judgment and teshuvah, and closes with chasing away a bad thought at once.

en: The beinoni is born to struggle with his yetzer hara until his last breath; this is his shlichus and that of most people.
A beinoni cannot control his heart's desires, but he can always control his action, speech and thought, doing and saying the opposite of what his heart wants and chasing away a bad thought.
Every aveira is like avodah zarah, and every Jew has a hidden love of Hashem that would make him give his life rather than serve an idol.
The beinoni overcomes temptation by telling himself that he does not want to be a rasha even for one moment, because in the chamber of his hidden love he truly hates evil.
Overcoming the yetzer hara every day is a true mesiras nefesh, since nefesh means one's will, and Hashem counts the sum total of these daily sacrifices.
A bad thought that comes into the mind is not an aveira; the aveira is letting it linger and exploring it, and the mitzvah is to chase it away at once.

title.en: The beinoni's lifelong struggle

summary.en: The Rav reviews the tzaddik and the rasha and opens chapter 14: the beinoni is born to struggle with his yetzer hara all his life, as most people are, and always wins the battle without killing the yetzer hara. He brings the Gemara that the yetzer hara is like a fly that keeps coming back.

title.en: The heart is not in his hands, deed, speech and thought are

summary.en: The Rav explains that every person can be a beinoni, and that having an urge to sin does not mean Hashem frowns on him; a stronger struggle may even come because he was raised to a higher level. The beinoni cannot control what his heart wants, but he can control his deeds, his speech and his thoughts, and say to himself that he does not want to be a rasha even for a moment.

title.en: Every aveira is avodah zarah; the hidden love

summary.en: The Rav recalls the earlier chapters: one who sins becomes a vessel for the sitra achra, worse than the lowliest creature because he has free choice, and the Ba'al Shem Tov said any deviation from Hashem's will is like avodah zarah. He explains why sin is called foolishness: every Jew, even the worst, has a hidden love that makes him ready to give his life rather than deny Anochi Hashem, which was heard directly from Hashem.

title.en: The thief who would not kiss the cross

summary.en: The Rav tells, from the sefer of Rabbi Yaakov Yosef, of a woman, by tradition Adel the daughter of the Ba'al Shem Tov, who said that Hashem did not make a bad choice in Klal Yisrael: a Jewish thief who had done every aveira was caught stealing from a church and let himself be burned rather than kiss the cross. He applies it to the Tanya: a person who sins would never sin if he knew that the aveira is also avodah zarah.

title.en: Daily struggle as mesiras nefesh

summary.en: Answering a listener who argues that dying once is easier than a lifetime of struggle, the Rav explains that nefesh means will, as Rashi explains, so resisting every day is mesiras nefesh, and Hashem counts its sum total, like a stone ground to sand that falls on a person grain by grain. He adds that only for the three cardinal sins must one give his life, because of v'chai bahem.

title.en: The advice: I do not want to be a rasha

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's advice: to tell one's heart that a rasha is a seat for the sitra achra, separated from Hashem. The tzaddik hates evil because he loves Hashem, as in 'ohavei Hashem sin'u ra'; the beinoni loves evil only on the surface, while in the chamber of his hidden love he hates it. Even the lowliest Jew can give his life for Kiddush Hashem, and he fails in the smaller test only because a spirit of folly makes him forget his hidden love.

title.en: The fortieth level and Yom Kippur

summary.en: The Rav explains that a person is made of forty levels, like the forty days of the forming of a child; a sinner gets thirty-nine lashes, not forty, because in the fortieth level he never sinned, and that is the hidden love. On Yom Kippur, the fortieth day, it surfaces and every Jew is forgiven, and this is how the Rambam explains why a forced 'I want' is true. He adds the strategy of delaying the urge and says a person always has the strength to overcome.

title.en: When bechirah is lost; Hashem looks inside

summary.en: Asked whether bechirah can be taken away, the Rav agrees it sometimes happens, as with Yehuda and Tamar and in the Gemara about a woman whose consent came after force, but only in isolated cases that Hashem knows; a person should always assume he still has bechirah. He says Hashem knows the inner self of every Jew, and Yom Kippur looks at that inner self, and teshuvah means returning to one's root, where one is good.

title.en: Levels of judgment, teshuvah and bad thoughts

summary.en: With the Yerushalmi on asking wisdom, Torah and Hashem what the sinner's punishment is, the Rav explains these are higher and higher levels, and Hashem judges by the inner will of a Jew; on this he reads the Rambam that the geulah comes through teshuvah. He closes with the Tanya's point that a bad thought is not a sin but an opportunity: one must chase it away at once and not explore it, so that the heart is in one's hands.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - Erev Pesach

oneLiner.en: At a bris just before Pesach, the Rav connects the child's entry into the covenant with Eliyahu Hanavi, who is present at the bris, announced on Shabbos Hagadol and awaited at the Seder, and with the rule that the Korban Pesach requires milah.

abstract.en: The Rav speaks at a bris shortly before Pesach. He notes that Chazal say Eliyahu Hanavi comes to every bris, that on Shabbos Hagadol the haftarah announces 'Behold I send you Eliyahu the prophet', and that Jews hold that Eliyahu comes to every Jewish home at the Seder. A bris within these few days thus joins Eliyahu, the bearer of good tidings, three times over, and the Rav calls it a good sign for the child. He blesses that Eliyahu, of whom it is said that the covenant was with him for life and peace, bring peace and the redemption, and that this seemingly private family simcha be the spark that ignites his coming. He then explains that milah is a central preparation for Pesach, since the Korban Pesach cannot be offered without it, and blesses that the child bring redemption to himself and to all of Klal Yisrael.

en: A bris just before Pesach links the child with Eliyahu Hanavi, who comes to the bris, is announced on Shabbos Hagadol and comes to the Seder.
The Rav calls it a good sign that the child entered the covenant of Avraham Avinu at a time when everyone awaits Eliyahu, the bearer of good tidings.
He asks that this family bris, seemingly a private matter, be the spark that ignites the coming of Eliyahu and the redemption.
Milah is one of the most important preparations for Pesach, since the Korban Pesach cannot be offered without it.

title.en: Eliyahu Hanavi and milah before Pesach

summary.en: The Rav links the bris with Eliyahu Hanavi, who comes to every bris, is announced on Shabbos Hagadol and comes to the Seder, and blesses that this family simcha be the spark that brings the redemption. He then explains that milah is a central preparation for Pesach, since the Korban Pesach cannot be offered without it, and blesses the child to bring redemption to all of Klal Yisrael.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Pesach, the Rav explains that Pesach, the head of the Yamim Tovim, binds Klal Yisrael to Hashem, that milah is a bond of its own, and that a bris on Pesach, with Eliyahu Hanavi present at both, is a bond upon a bond.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Rambam in Sefer Hamitzvos: the month can be sanctified only in Eretz Yisrael, so without Jews settled there there would be no Yamim Tovim, and that would be the destruction of Klal Yisrael. The three Regalim are thus the existence of the nation, and Pesach is the head of them all. Citing the Chiddushei HaRim, he explains that Pesach alone carries kareis, for chametz and for not bringing the Korban Pesach, a sign that its mitzvos bind Jews to Hashem; and eating the Korban Pesach requires milah, another bond. Milah too carries kareis, so a bris on Pesach is a bond upon a bond. Eliyahu Hanavi, who turns the hearts of fathers to sons, comes both at Pesach and at a bris, and hearing good tidings is a time of favor for renewal. He closes with blessings for the redemption.

en: According to the Rambam, the Yamim Tovim depend on sanctifying the month in Eretz Yisrael, and the three Regalim are the existence of Klal Yisrael.
Pesach is the head of all the Yamim Tovim and establishes the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisrael.
The kareis attached to Pesach's mitzvos shows that they bind a Jew to Hashem, and milah, required for the Korban Pesach, is a further bond.
A bris on Pesach is a bond upon a bond, and Eliyahu Hanavi, who binds Jews to Hashem, comes to both.

bond between Klal Yisrael and Hashem

title.en: Pesach and milah as a double bond

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam that the Yamim Tovim, headed by Pesach, are the existence of Klal Yisrael, and explains from the kareis of Pesach's mitzvos and the milah needed for the Korban Pesach that Pesach binds Jews to Hashem. A bris on Pesach, with Eliyahu Hanavi present at both, is a bond upon a bond, and he closes with blessings for the redemption.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Chol Hamoed Pesach, the Rav explains that milah, the removal of the orlah, is a person's own removal of chametz and a model of the removal of impurity from the world that Pesach and the days of Moshiach bring.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by noting that Pesach is a time of Eliyahu Hanavi, announced on Shabbos Hagadol, when Jews await the great salvation. Pesach nullifies the kelipos, the forces of evil, through removing chametz, and a person's own removal is the bris milah that removes the orlah; the Torah requires milah to eat the Korban Pesach. Each bris awakens the days of Moshiach and is a model of removing the spirit of impurity from the land. Avraham Avinu's war with the four kings on Pesach, he says, was against the four layers of the orlah, the four kelipos. Pesach and milah are the only positive mitzvos carrying kareis, and the Chiddushei HaRim says the reverse of kareis is a bond with Hashem, so a bris on Pesach is especially in its time. He explains why Aleinu is said after a bris, and closes with blessings.

en: Pesach nullifies the kelipos through removing chametz, and bris milah, removing the orlah, is a person's own removal.
Every bris awakens the days of Moshiach and is a model of removing the spirit of impurity from the land.
Avraham Avinu's war with the four kings on Pesach corresponds to the four layers of the orlah, the four kelipos.
Pesach and milah alone among positive mitzvos carry kareis, and since the reverse of kareis is a bond with Hashem, a bris on Pesach is especially in its time.

candidateTopics: Avraham Avinu and the four kings
spirit of impurity removed from the land

title.en: Milah as removing the orlah on Pesach

summary.en: The Rav compares the bris to the removal of chametz, explains that milah is a model of removing impurity from the world and ties the four layers of the orlah to Avraham Avinu's war with the four kings on Pesach. From the kareis shared by Pesach and milah he concludes that a bris on Pesach is especially in its time, explains why Aleinu is said after a bris, and closes with blessings.

catalogTitle: בינוני הוא עובד ה'- צדיק הוא עבד ה'. מדריגות בבינוני - עובד ה'' ואשר לא עבדו.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the beinoni's avodah is measured by his toil rather than his feelings, and that by striving to act like a tzaddik he can draw down the soul of a tzaddik to help him.

abstract.en: Continuing the Tanya's discussion of the beinoni, the Rav distinguishes avodas avodah, serving Hashem with toil and without desire, from avodas matanah, the gift of enjoying one's service given to tzaddikim. He shows from Avraham Avinu at the Akeidah, who acted without any feeling, that toil is the essence of avodah, and describes Shabbos as a time when many taste the gift, telling stories of tzaddikim who sought the Shabbos within the food. He then answers the Tanya's opening question about the oath to be a tzaddik: some are born tzaddikim, depending on the root of their souls in Adam Harishon, and the oath obligates everyone at least to strive. The beinoni should meditate on how fleeting worldly pleasure is and on Hashem's greatness, training himself until it becomes second nature. Such effort sets corresponding forces above vibrating, and the soul of a tzaddik may come as an ibbur to help him.

en: Avodas avodah, serving Hashem through toil without desire, is the essence of a person's avodah; avodas matanah, enjoying the service, is a gift given to tzaddikim.
Avraham Avinu performed the Akeidah, the greatest mitzvah ever done, with his spiritual levels taken from him and without feeling, showing that avodah is measured by effort, not by feeling.
Some are born tzaddikim, depending on where their soul is rooted in Adam Harishon, while others must struggle not to be a rasha.
The oath to be a tzaddik obligates even a beinoni who cannot reach that level to strive for it, by setting times to meditate on Hashem's greatness and the emptiness of worldly pleasure.
Through practice the beinoni's joy in Hashem becomes second nature, though it is not the tzaddik's true nature.
A person who strives to act like a tzaddik can become a dwelling for the soul of a tzaddik that comes as an ibbur, and through it serve Hashem with true joy.

roots of souls in Adam Harishon

title.en: Avodas avodah and the Akeidah

summary.en: The Rav reviews that the beinoni cannot control the inclinations of his heart and that tzaddikim have levels. He distinguishes avodas avodah, toil without desire, from avodas matanah, the gift of enjoying the service, and shows from Avraham Avinu at the Akeidah that avodah is measured by effort, not feeling.

title.en: Shabbos, a taste of the gift

summary.en: The Rav explains that at special times, above all Shabbos, and after overcoming a test, Hashem lets a person taste the pleasure of Olam Haba. He tells of a poor young tzaddik who asked for Shabbos in his challah and fish, and of a chassid who said a poritz's lavish sugar spectacle could not compare to his pleasure saying Nishmas on Shabbos, while noting that not everyone merits it.

title.en: Born tzaddikim and the roots of souls

summary.en: The Rav returns to the Tanya's opening question about the oath to be a tzaddik and explains that Hashem created tzaddikim: some are born tzaddikim, as in the mashal of children born on a mountaintop. He explains that this depends on where a soul is rooted in Adam Harishon, in the head for Torah or the heart for tefillah.

title.en: The beinoni must still strive

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's answer: the oath tells everyone to strive to be a tzaddik and at least not to be a rasha. The beinoni should set times to think about how fleeting worldly pleasures are and about Hashem's greatness in caring for him, bringing himself to joy in Hashem even if it is only imitation, and try even if he may never reach it.

title.en: Second nature and the tuning fork

summary.en: The Rav explains that through practice the beinoni's joy becomes second nature, like someone who trains himself to walk on his hands, and that the Tanya calls it truth according to his level rather than absolute truth. With the mashal of a piano tuner's tuning fork he explains that an act below sets the corresponding forces above vibrating, bringing a response from above.

title.en: Gilgulim and the decrees of persecution

summary.en: The Rav digresses on gilgul, explaining that it answers why tzaddikim suffer. He tells that those killed in the Chmielnicki decrees were explained as the souls of those who worshipped idols in Nevuchadnetzar's time, for whom the decree of Haman was nullified, alluded to by the large ches and tav in the Megillah.

title.en: The ibbur of a tzaddik's soul

summary.en: The Rav explains ibbur, when a tzaddik's soul temporarily dwells in another Jew, and tells of a talmid who merited the soul of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair through pidyon shvuyim. He explains that a beinoni who strives hard sets the heavenly chords vibrating and may become a seat for a tzaddik's soul, serving with true joy, and mentions that Moshe Rabbeinu comes down once in fifty years in a tzaddik's soul.

title.en: The lasting mark of an ibbur

summary.en: After a brief personal note, the Rav adds that a born tzaddik earned it through a previous gilgul, and that an ibbur may last a moment or a lifetime but always leaves a mark of kedushah and an incentive to reach that level again. He answers a question briefly and closes with wishes for the summer.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Shavuos is fixed by the counting of every Jew rather than by Beis Din's calendar, because every Jew holds the Torah as an inheritance and can become a great talmid chacham, and he blesses the child at the bris to realize that potential.

abstract.en: At a bris during Sefirah, the Rav notes that the other festivals depend on Beis Din, on the sanctifying of the month and the leap year. Shavuos alone has no fixed date; it falls fifty days after Pesach, set by the counting. Following the Chasam Sofer, he asks why the Torah tied Shavuos to counting. He answers that every Jew holds the Torah as an inheritance in his soul, so even a simple Jew carries the potential to be, or to raise, a great talmid chacham. Since every Jew counts, every Jew fixes the day of the giving of the Torah, showing that each is a 'master of the house' in Torah. He connects this to the bris, where the child receives the powers of his soul, and blesses him to grow into a great talmid chacham and to receive the Torah on Shavuos.

en: Shavuos is fixed by counting fifty days from Pesach, not by a calendar date set through Beis Din's sanctifying of the month.
Every Jew holds the Torah as an inheritance in his soul, so every Jew carries the potential of a talmid chacham.
Because the counting belongs to every single Jew, every Jew takes part in fixing the time of the giving of the Torah.
At the bris the child receives the powers of his soul, which he can develop into greatness in Torah and yiras Shamayim.

every Jew a potential talmid chacham

title.en: Shavuos fixed by everyone's counting, and the bris

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the festivals fixed by Beis Din's sanctifying of the month with Shavuos, which falls fifty days after Pesach by the counting, and asks with the Chasam Sofer why. He answers that every Jew inherits the Torah and carries the potential of a great talmid chacham, so every Jew, by counting, fixes the day of the giving of the Torah. He then applies this to the bris and blesses the child to grow into a great talmid chacham and receive the Torah on Shavuos.

title.en: Singing

summary.en: Singing after the drashah; the transcript holds only fragments of song.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Parshas Kedoshim, the Rav brings a vort of the Chasam Sofer that Shabbos and the festivals are a Jew's father and mother, and gathers the reasons for joy: the parsha, the day of Sefirah and the bris itself.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a vort of the Chasam Sofer: the first letters of the passuk about Moshe telling the festivals of Hashem to the Jewish people spell 'my mother' and 'my father', because Shabbos and the festivals are a Jew's father and mother, who teach him and instill good middos, as parents do for a child. He says he wanted to repeat it because the souls of forebears come to a simcha, and a descendant of the Chasam Sofer is at this bris. He then recalls that the companions of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai rejoiced at Parshas Kedoshim, on which most of the Torah depends, since a Jew rejoices in whatever brings him closeness to Hashem. A bris brings that closeness, and this one coincides with Kedoshim, with a day of Sefirah linked to milah, and with the day's word in Lamenatzeach, 'yismechu'. He closes with blessings of joy for the parents, for Klal Yisrael and for the redemption.

en: Shabbos and the festivals are a Jew's father and mother, teaching him and giving him good middos.
The companions of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai rejoiced when Parshas Kedoshim was read.
A Jew rejoices in what brings him closeness to Hashem, and every bris brings such closeness.
This bris joins several joys: the parsha, the day of Sefirah, the day's word 'yismechu', and the bris itself.

candidateTopics: Shabbos and the festivals as parents

title.en: Shabbos as father and mother; joy of Kedoshim and the bris

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer's vort that Shabbos and the festivals are a Jew's father and mother, recalls the joy of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's companions at Parshas Kedoshim, and connects the bris to the parsha, the day of Sefirah and its word 'yismechu', ending with blessings for the parents and Klal Yisrael.

catalogTitle: עבודה תמה זהו שבירת היצר. שלא לחפוש מנוחה - זהו עבודת אברהם אוהבי. שייכות ענין זה למילה.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's distinction between the 'oved Elokim', the beinoni who keeps fighting his yetzer hara, and the one who 'has not served Him' because his good conduct costs him no struggle, and stresses that for the beinoni this lifelong struggle is a complete avodah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens Tanya chapter 15 with the verse in Malachi that contrasts tzaddik with rasha and 'oved Elokim' with 'one who has not served Him'. 'Oved' is present tense: the beinoni who is still at war with the yetzer hara over the 'small city' of the body, while 'eved', a noun, is the tzaddik who has already won. He digresses on how much weaker today's generation is, comparing it to a small child whose slips are forgiven, and supports this with the yetzer hara cited before and after the Flood and with Bilaam's blessing that Hashem does not look at wrongdoing in Yaakov. He then defines the beinoni 'who has not served Him': a natural or habituated masmid who does no aveiros but makes no effort beyond his routine, explained through the Gemara of learning a hundred versus a hundred and one times. The beinoni's lifelong struggle is a complete avodah, illustrated by two stories.

en: Tzaddik and rasha form one pair and 'oved Elokim' and 'one who has not served Him' a second pair, both within the level of the beinoni and the tzaddik who is not a rasha.

'Oved' in the present tense describes the beinoni who is in the middle of the war with the yetzer hara, while 'eved', a noun like 'chacham' or 'melech', describes the tzaddik who has already driven it out.
The beinoni 'who has not served Him' does no aveiros and learns constantly, but does it by routine, without fighting his yetzer hara or striving to grow.
Such a person may be a natural masmid, cooled by the black gall, or one who trained himself until learning became second nature; either way he needs only the hidden love of Hashem every Jew has.
Learning a hundred and one times, one more than the accustomed hundred, is what makes one an 'oved Elokim', because it breaks a routine.
For the beinoni, the constant struggle against the yetzer hara until his last breath is a complete avodah; Hashem does not demand that he become a tzaddik.

the yetzer hara and the Flood

title.en: Oved Elokim versus eved

summary.en: The Rav opens the chapter with the verse contrasting tzaddik and rasha, oved Elokim and one who has not served Him, and explains that 'oved' is the beinoni still at war with the yetzer hara while 'eved' is the tzaddik who has already won. He then notes that the beinoni himself has two levels.

title.en: A weaker generation, treated gently

summary.en: The Rav digresses on how far the world has fallen since earlier generations, recalling the decent world of his youth, and says that today one must be gentler with talmidim and friends. Like a two-year-old who slips, today's Jews are not held to the old standard; what matters is that they want to do Hashem's will.

title.en: The yetzer hara before and after the Flood

summary.en: The Rav asks how the yetzer hara could be the reason both for bringing the Flood and for never bringing another, and answers that the mighty generations before it were held responsible while the weakened world after it is treated like a sick child. He adds Bilaam's blessing that Hashem does not look at wrongdoing in Yaakov, with Rashi, and distinguishes one who slips while wanting to be good from one who sins in rebellion.

title.en: The beinoni who has not served Him

summary.en: The Rav defines the beinoni 'who has not served Him': he keeps all the mitzvos and learns constantly but by routine, without using Hashem's help to grow. He explains why such a person needs no struggle: he is a natural masmid of cold temperament, or he trained himself until it became second nature, so the hidden love of Hashem suffices.

title.en: A hundred and one times

summary.en: The Rav explains the Gemara that one who reviews a hundred times has not served Him, while one who reviews a hundred and one times has: like the donkey drivers who charge double past the usual distance, the extra time goes beyond the routine. He links a hundred to the gematria of the yetzer hara's name and a hundred and one to the angel Michael, and concludes that the beinoni must always seek to grow, which is his complete avodah.

title.en: The struggle until the last breath

summary.en: Few people kill the yetzer hara; most struggle until their last moment. The Rav tells of a chassid who on his deathbed made a gesture of victory over the yetzer hara, and the Chiddushei HaRim's comment that at that moment he lost the battle. This lifelong struggle is the beinoni's complete avodah.

title.en: The masmid of Koretz and his judgment

summary.en: The Rav tells of a young masmid in Koretz who agreed to divorce rather than stop learning, was brought back by his father-in-law, and after his death reported that he was sentenced to Gehinnom for one fleeting proud thought, a sentence reduced because he accepted it without question. He concludes that if people today were judged this way it would be grim, but the main thing is to truly want to be an oved, and Hashem does not scrutinize those who slip.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the festivals and the mitzvah of milah lift a Jew above the level of the tribes to the root of the Avos, and sees a sign in a bris that falls in the week of Parshas Emor, with its chapter of the festivals.

abstract.en: The Rav describes the Avos as the trunk of the tree and the tribes as its branches. Each tribe has its own portion in Eretz Yisrael, and the mitzvos are spread over the land, but some things stand above the tribes, such as Yerushalayim. The three festivals correspond to Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, so when Jews go up to Yerushalayim, where the tribes ascend, they rise above their tribal root to the root of the Avos. Milah too is above the tribes: it is the covenant of Avraham Avinu, and after his milah Hashem appeared to him, a revelation of 'seeing' tied to the command that every male appear on the festivals. A bris in the week of Parshas Emor, with its chapter of the festivals, is therefore a sign of an elevated bris that binds all present to the Avos. He blesses the child to enter Torah, chuppah and good deeds, and that his merit join that of Klal Yisrael.

en: The Avos are the trunk of the tree and the tribes are its branches, each with its own portion in Eretz Yisrael.
The three festivals correspond to the Avos, so on them Jews rise above the root of the tribes to the root of the Avos.
Milah is above the tribes; it is the covenant of Avraham Avinu and binds to the root of the Avos.
A bris in the week of the festivals' chapter is a sign of an elevated bris that binds everyone present to the Avos.

title.en: Milah and the festivals: above the tribes

summary.en: The Rav explains that the tribes are branches of the Avos, that the festivals and the going up to Yerushalayim lift Jews to the root of the Avos, and that milah, the covenant of Avraham, does the same. He sees the bris in the week of Parshas Emor as a sign of an elevated bris and closes with blessings for the child and the family.

oneLiner.en: At a bris of twins on Yesod shebeMalchus, the Rav explains that this day of the Omer completes the tikkun of Yesod, a sign that the child is prepared to become a tzaddik, and ties the twins to the mazal of Sivan and Matan Torah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by mentioning the custom not to take a haircut during the days of Sefiras HaOmer and how practice differs between places. He notes that there is a deeper reason, but in simple terms one can explain that by Yesod shebeMalchus the Omer count has already passed through the Yesod of every middah, so the whole tikkun of Yesod is complete. A bris, which is in Yesod, held on Yesod shebeMalchus is therefore a good sign that the child is prepared to be a tzaddik and to grow in Torah and yiras Shamayim. It is also a great preparation for Matan Torah. Since this is a bris of twins, the Rav adds that the mazal of the month of Sivan, the month of receiving the Torah, is te'omim, twins, as the Bnei Yissaschar and other sefarim bring. He closes with brachos for the children and the parents.

en: By Yesod shebeMalchus the Omer count has passed through the Yesod of every middah, so the tikkun of Yesod is complete.
A bris, which is in Yesod, on Yesod shebeMalchus is a sign that the child is prepared to become a great tzaddik.
A bris on this day is a great preparation for Matan Torah.
The mazal of Sivan, the month of receiving the Torah, is twins, which makes a bris of twins on this day especially fitting.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Emor, the Rav explains why the parsha of the kohanim is the parsha Eliyahu HaNavi will expound, and connects it to Eliyahu at every bris and to a young father who held fast to Yiddishkeit.

abstract.en: The Rav begins with the week's haftorah from Yechezkel about the kohanim, the bnei Tzadok, who kept Hashem's charge when the rest of Yisrael strayed; they kept up the Jewish mesorah, and they will be the ones who draw close to Hashem in the days of Moshiach. The haftorah ends with the prohibition for kohanim to eat neveilah and treifah, and the Gemara asks why kohanim are singled out; Rabbi Yochanan answers that Eliyahu will expound this parsha. The Rav explains that at the geulah the spirit of impurity will be removed and even forbidden things will become kosher, as the Midrash says of the chazir, but the kohanim, as higher Jews, will still not eat them. Every Jew has his own letter in the Torah, and Emor is Eliyahu's parsha. Eliyahu, the kohen tzedek and malach habris, comes to every bris, so a bris in Emor for a young father who fought for Yiddishkeit is a special segulah. He closes with brachos.

en: The kohanim, bnei Tzadok, kept Hashem's charge and the Jewish mesorah when the rest of Yisrael strayed, and they will draw close to Hashem in the days of Moshiach.
Eliyahu will expound the parsha of neveilah and treifah for kohanim because at the geulah even forbidden things will become kosher, yet the kohanim will still not eat them.
Every Jew has his own letter in the Torah, where his learning shines and his chiddushim come, and Emor is Eliyahu's parsha.
A bris in the week of Emor, for a young father who fought for Yiddishkeit, is a special segulah, since Eliyahu, the kohen tzedek and malach habris, comes to every bris.

He closes with brachos to hear Eliyahu's derasha at the geulah.

oneLiner.en: Opening Tanya chapter 16, the Rav explains that a Jew's service is to rule over nature, shown by Avraham's inherited emunah above understanding and by the mitzvah of milah, and made possible by the neshamah that stands above nature.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews the end of Tanya chapter 15: true service of Hashem is the effort to go beyond routine, aroused either by contemplating Hashem's greatness or by stirring the hidden love inherited from Avraham Avinu. Opening chapter 16, which calls for ruling over the nature in the left chamber of the heart, he ties this to milah. A Jew's emunah is hereditary, like an animal's instinct, while a non-Jew is held responsible because an honest look at the world and at Sinai shows the truth. Avraham was a new species, given a new power of birth through the added hei. His mitzvos were emunah and milah: emunah begins where understanding ends, so milah comes at eight days, while Yishmael's empty milah waits for thirteen. After a long digression on Yishmael, Eretz Yisrael and the end of the exile, he returns: milah defies nature, and the neshamah, above nature, lets the mind rule the heart.

en: True service of Hashem is the effort that breaks routine and comfort, aroused either by contemplating Hashem's greatness or by stirring the hidden love in the heart.
A Jew's emunah is an inheritance from Avraham Avinu, hereditary like an animal's instinct, while a non-Jew is held responsible because honest observation of the world and of Sinai leads to the truth.
Emunah begins where understanding ends, and milah at eight days is the sign of this emunah above understanding.
Milah is the clearest illustration of a Jew's task to defy nature: right at birth one removes what nature produced.
A person can rule over nature because his neshamah, a part of G-d above, is above nature and shines into his nefesh, so the mind rules over the heart.

signs of the coming of Moshiach

title.en: Review: what makes one an oved Hashem

summary.en: The Rav reviews that real service of Hashem is the extra effort beyond routine, and the two ways the Tanya gives to arouse it: contemplating Hashem's greatness, or stirring the hidden love inherited from Avraham Avinu.

title.en: Chapter 16: ruling nature; inherited emunah

summary.en: The Rav opens chapter 16, that the main thing is to rule over nature, and links it to milah and to the emunah inherited from Avraham. He compares hereditary emunah to animal instinct and explains why a non-Jew is still responsible to believe.

title.en: Avraham, a new species of believer

summary.en: The Rav explains that a non-Jew's denial is rationalization to escape obligation, while Jews believe by inheritance. Avraham and Sarah were barren because Avraham was a new species, given a new power of birth with the added hei, and with him creation was completed.

title.en: Emunah and milah: above understanding

summary.en: After a question about Yishmael, the Rav explains that Avraham's mitzvos are emunah and milah. Emunah starts where understanding ends, which is why milah is done at eight days without daas, while Yishmael's milah at thirteen is an empty milah that needs daas.

title.en: The eighth day and Yishmael's empty milah

summary.en: The Rav explains that milah is on the eighth day because the senses and intellect reach only the nature of the seven days of creation, while Jewish emunah is above nature. Yishmael's milah lacks the spiritual power of a Jew's, and the Zohar says he received Eretz Yisrael through it while it lies empty.

title.en: Digression: Yishmael and the end of exile

summary.en: In a long digression the Rav speaks of Eretz Yisrael flourishing as a sign of Moshiach, of Yishmael as the adversary of Yitzchak and the last stage of the exile, and of Torah codes he heard from Rav Michoel Ber Weissmandl, pointing to a hint of Moshiach in this week's parsha.

title.en: Milah: the model of breaking nature

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Rav explains that nature dictates every creature's behavior and a Jew must rule above it. Milah removes the orlah that nature produces, and that power accompanies a Jew all his life: to get up when nature says sleep, and to check and sanctify himself even in what is permitted.

title.en: How a creature of nature rules nature

summary.en: The Rav asks how a person, himself a product of nature, can defy it, and answers from the Tanya that the neshamah, a part of G-d above, shines into the nefesh, so the mind rules the heart. Contemplating Hashem's greatness in chochmah and binah gives birth to the middos and to withdrawing from evil.

oneLiner.en: At a bris, the Rav explains that being counted by Moshe Rabbeinu, like being seen by Eliyahu HaNavi at a bris, is itself a great blessing, and that the last, fallen generation of 'Bnei Naftali' is helped from Above when it serves Hashem with mesiras nefesh.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the week's parsha: every tribe is counted 'livnei', with a lamed, except Naftali. He brings the Chasam Sofer: since Naftali was counted last, its number was already known, so its count served only the purpose the Ramban describes, that each Jew came before Moshe and Aharon to be seen and blessed. He then explains why Eliyahu HaNavi comes to every bris: a father who cuts his own child with joy needs help from Above, and Eliyahu, who was moser nefesh for the bris in the episode of Zimri, comes to help. Being seen by him is a great good, like being seen by Moshe. The child is named after Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. Our generation, the last and 'fallen' one, is Bnei Naftali, and whoever holds on to Torah with mesiras nefesh is helped by Hashem. He closes with blessings.

en: Naftali's count lacks the lamed because, as the last tribe, its number was already known, so it was counted only so that its people would come before Moshe Rabbeinu and be blessed.
Being counted by Moshe and Aharon was a great good for each Jew: Moshe looked at him, asked how he was doing and blessed him.
Eliyahu HaNavi comes to every bris to help the father, who needs great strength and help from Above to cut his own child with joy.
Whoever wants to serve Hashem is helped: angels and souls of tzaddikim come to help him, and above all Hashem Himself.
Our generation, the last one, is 'Bnei Naftali', a fallen generation in which holding on to Torah and mitzvos takes mesiras nefesh, and Hashem helps whoever does so.

help from Above in serving Hashem

title.en: Why Naftali is counted without a lamed

summary.en: The Rav notes that in the parsha's census every tribe is counted 'livnei' except Naftali. He brings the Chasam Sofer and the Ramban: Naftali's number was already known, so it was counted only so that its people would come before Moshe Rabbeinu, be looked at and blessed.

title.en: Why Eliyahu HaNavi comes to every bris

summary.en: The Rav explains that a father who cuts his child with joy needs help from Above, and Eliyahu, who was moser nefesh for the holiness of the bris in the episode of Zimri, comes to help. Being seen by Eliyahu is a great good, like being seen by Moshe; he blesses the child to enter Torah, chuppah and good deeds with the same mesiras nefesh and joy.

title.en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the last generation, and blessings

summary.en: The child is named after Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, and the Rav brings the Midrash Pinchas that the soul whose name is given comes to the bris. He explains that the last generation is Bnei Naftali, a fallen generation, and that whoever holds on to Torah in it with mesiras nefesh receives help from Above, and closes with blessings for the child, the family and all present.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in Sivan, the Rav distinguishes two brissos, Hashem's covenant of the soul with Avraham and the bris milah that is its sign, and explains that in Sivan, the month of Matan Torah, the covenant between Klal Yisrael and Hashem is strengthened.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a Midrash that in Megillas Rus every passuk but eight begins with a vav, hinting that Rus accepted the mitzvah of milah. He notes that Avraham received his new name before his milah, though a name is usually given after it. To explain, he distinguishes two brissos: first, Hashem's covenant with Avraham, a bond of the neshamah that ties every Jew to Hashem and does not depend on the flesh, as the Mishnah in Nedarim says that a Jew is called circumcised even if he is not, and a non-Jew uncircumcised even if he is; for this Avraham received his name. Afterwards came the os bris, the bris milah, as a sign of that covenant. A woman shares in the first bris, and that is what Rus took on. A bris in Sivan, when Klal Yisrael came to Sinai and their covenant with Hashem was strengthened, is a great chizuk to feel bound to Hashem, like Avraham, the first of the believers. He closes with brachos.

en: There are two brissos: Hashem's covenant with Avraham, a bond of the neshamah, and the bris milah, which is its sign.
The covenant of the neshamah does not depend on the flesh: a Jew is called circumcised even if he is not, and a non-Jew uncircumcised even if he is.
Avraham received his name for the first covenant, which is why it came before his milah.
A woman also belongs to the covenant of Avraham, and this is what Rus accepted, as hinted by the eight pesukim that do not begin with a vav.
In Sivan, when Yisrael came to Sinai, their covenant with Hashem was strengthened, so a bris in Sivan is a great chizuk to feel bound to Hashem.

title.en: Avraham's name and the covenant of the soul

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Rus accepted milah, asks why Avraham was named before his milah, and answers with two brissos: a covenant of the neshamah that binds every Jew to Hashem regardless of the flesh, as the Mishnah in Nedarim shows, and the later os bris in the flesh.

title.en: Rus, Sivan and strengthening the covenant

summary.en: The Rav explains that Rus took on the covenant of Avraham, which a woman shares, and that a bris in Sivan, when Yisrael's covenant with Hashem was strengthened at Sinai, is a chizuk to feel bound to Hashem like Avraham, the first of the believers; he closes with brachos.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Shavuos the Rav explains, from the end of Megillas Rus, why Oved was given that name: he carried a difficult heritage that he had to refine through hard work, and that is the blessing given to the newborn child.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the blessing in Megillas Rus, 'vayikarei shemo b'Yisrael', which the Targum reads as a wish that the child be counted among the tzaddikim of Israel, and a Midrash that the last eight pesukim of the megillah correspond to the bris on the eighth day. He asks why the megillah repeats the genealogy from Peretz after naming Oved as the grandfather of Dovid. Bringing the Arizal, he explains that Oved carried the soul of Machlon, returned through yibum, and before that the history of Er through Peretz. This is why he was called Oved: the Targum says he served Hashem with a whole heart, but many did that; Oved had to work hard on himself to refine what he was born with. Rus, too, labored all her life on her traits, which is why the neighbors named the child. The Rav ends with the eighth day, above nature, its link to Shavuos, and blessings for the child.

en: The blessing 'vayikarei shemo b'Yisrael' at the end of Megillas Rus is, per the Targum, a wish that the child be among the tzaddikim of Israel, and it was said at Oved's bris.
Oved carried the soul of Machlon, brought back through yibum, and through Peretz also the history of Er, which needed rectifying.
He was called Oved because he had to work hard on himself to refine what he was born with, unlike a tzaddik who serves Hashem easily out of a good heart.
Rus, born a daughter of the king of Moav, labored all her life to refine her traits, and the neighbors named the child because she would not, remembering her past.
Milah on the eighth day is above nature, which runs in sevens, and it is linked to the Torah given as the eighth week begins.

title.en: Oved's bris and the souls of Machlon and Er

summary.en: The Rav opens with 'vayikarei shemo b'Yisrael', the Targum's reading of it, and a Midrash tying the megillah's last eight pesukim to the bris on the eighth day. He asks why the genealogy from Peretz is repeated and brings the Arizal that Oved carried the soul of Machlon through yibum, and that Er stood behind Peretz.

title.en: Why he was called Oved

summary.en: The Rav asks, with the Targum that Oved served Hashem with a whole heart, why only he was called by that name. He answers that the histories of Machlon and Peretz merged in him, so he had to work hard on himself, and this made him the forebear of Yishai; milah, too, removes the bad a person is born with.

title.en: Rus, the neighbors' name, and the eighth day

summary.en: The Rav explains that Rus labored all her life to refine her traits, so she would not name the child, and the neighbors comforted her and blessed him to be an oved. He ties milah on the eighth day, above nature, to the Torah given at Shavuos, and ends with blessings for the child.

catalogTitle: אהבה ויראה שכליות מביאה את האדם לתשובה. רשע ורע לו אין לו אפשרות להיות עובד ה' אלא ע"י תשובה תתאה.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains how a beinoni whose heart cannot be stirred to feel love of Hashem can still serve Him through love and fear that he understands with his mind, and how Hashem joins that intellectual love to his mitzvos so they rise above.

abstract.en: The Rav reads the opening of Tanya chapter 16: the great rule for a beinoni is that the mind rules the heart, so that contemplating Hashem's greatness arouses love and fear. Most people, however, understand but cannot feel; the Tanya's note traces this to a soul still in the stage of 'ibur', not yet 'born'. Such a person still understands that his soul should long to leave the body and cleave to Hashem, like a 'living widow' kept from her husband, and that the only contact is Torah and mitzvos. The Rav brings stories of souls nearly leaving the body in dveikus, and the principle of 'ratzo vashov'. Acting on this intellectual love gives the mitzvos the two wings of love and fear. Since thought is too high to clothe a physical deed, Hashem 'combines' it with the deed beyond nature, as Chazal say of a good thought, lifting such mitzvos to the world of Beriah.

en: The Rav explains the rule for the beinoni: action should flow from the mind, which contemplates Hashem's greatness and sends its message down to arouse love and fear in the heart.
Most people cannot turn understanding into felt love, because their soul is from the stage of 'ibur', still hidden like a fetus and not yet revealed.
Such a person still understands that his soul, sent down from the Kisei HaKavod, is like a 'living widow' longing for her husband, and that its only contact with Hashem is through Torah and mitzvos.
When he does mitzvos because of this intellectual love and fear, they act as the two wings that lift the mitzvos above, as if he felt real love.
By nature, love that is only in the mind cannot be the shliach of a physical deed, since only the heart is both physical and spiritual; Hashem combines it with the deed beyond nature.
Mitzvos done by habit, with no love or fear even in the mind, stop in a lower world, while those done with intellectual love and fear reach the world of Beriah.

title.en: The mind should rule the heart

summary.en: The Rav reads the opening of the chapter, the great rule for the beinoni that the mind directs the heart. He contrasts a 'seichel nivdal', an intellect untouched by emotion, with the common case where laziness bends the mind to justify putting off davening.

title.en: Those who understand but cannot feel

summary.en: The Rav describes the desired path, where the mind's contemplation stimulates love of Hashem in the heart, and says most people cannot reach it. He explains that souls pass through stages like conception, pregnancy and birth, and a soul sent down before its 'birth' cannot produce felt love, so it serves Hashem from understanding alone.

title.en: Love hidden in the mind: the soul of ibur

summary.en: Reading the Tanya, the Rav explains that such a person's love stays hidden and never flames in the heart. The Tanya's note gives the reason: his soul is from the stage of 'ibur', not yet revealed. Still he understands that his soul should long to leave the body and cleave to Hashem.

title.en: Ratzo vashov: souls that nearly flew out

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem made the world run on 'ratzo vashov', running and returning, so no one may let his soul rush out in love. He tells of a tzaddik who played with his pocket watch in Shemoneh Esrei to keep his soul in his body, and brings a sefer that Avraham's words 'we will return' kept his soul in him at the Akeidah, while Sarah's soul left her when she heard of it.

title.en: The soul as a 'living widow'

summary.en: The Rav explains that the soul, which comes from the Kisei HaKavod, is held in the body against its will like a 'living widow' whose husband is alive but barriers keep her from him. He adds that in galus the tzaddikim long for Hashem more than in the time of the Beis HaMikdash, like a thirsty man in the desert without water.

title.en: Torah and mitzvos: the only contact

summary.en: The Rav explains that the soul in the body can grasp Hashem only through Torah and mitzvos, citing the earlier chapters' parable of one who embraces the king through his garments. One who understands this with his mind, and makes his mouth and limbs act on it, gives his mitzvos wings even without felt love.

title.en: The two wings and the Ba'al Shem Tov's shul

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that love and fear are the two wings that lift mitzvos, and tells of the Ba'al Shem Tov who could not enter a shul packed with mitzvos done without love and fear. He explains that intellectual love counts as these wings, which is why Chassidus dwells so much on the greatness of Hashem, and that without it a person would follow his body's pleasures.

title.en: Why 'combines' it with the deed

summary.en: The Rav brings Chazal that Hashem combines a good thought with the deed, and asks why they did not simply say He credits it as if it were done. He explains that felt love and fear give the mitzvah life because the heart is a physical organ that also holds spiritual emotion, so it can be the shliach of the limbs, as the Gemara shows from the kohanim as shluchim of Hashem.

title.en: Why the mind cannot be the shliach

summary.en: Reading the Tanya, the Rav explains that the heart, physical like the other limbs yet inward, can carry love and fear into the deed. Love that stays in the mind is far higher than the deed and cannot clothe it, so by nature it could not lift the mitzvah; it does so only because Hashem combines it.

title.en: Hashem joins thought to deed

summary.en: The Rav answers the question: Hashem, Who can do anything, goes beyond nature and joins the intellectual love to the deed, as the Rema explains that He joins the spiritual soul to the physical body. Mitzvos done this way reach the world of Beriah, while mitzvos done by rote, with the mind on business, go up only to a lower world.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Rosh Chodesh Tamuz the Rav explains that, as milah removes the orlah to reveal the holiness beneath, the dark days of Tamuz hide great light, and contrasts milah, holiness above understanding, with tefillin, the peak of understanding.

abstract.en: The Rav notes that the bris falls on Rosh Chodesh Tamuz, at the start of the period that the navi says will turn into days of joy. Everything in the soul exists in time: the bris kodesh is the greatest holiness, covered by an orlah, and a Jew's work is to remove it; so too Tamuz, the brightest month, is covered, and through toil in Torah and avodah one finds the Shechinah 'bein hametzarim'. Sefer Yetzirah links Tamuz to the letter ches, the first ches in the Torah is choshech, darkness, and Tamuz with its milui equals 'yehi or'. A child circumcised on such a day is suited to reveal that light. From the Gemara on 'sasson' as milah and 'yekar' as tefillin, he explains milah as holiness above daas, given before a child understands, and tefillin as the peak of daas. Everyone at a bris should take this to heart, and he closes with blessings for redemption.

en: Just as the holiness of the bris is covered by an orlah that must be removed, the bright month of Tamuz is covered, and its light is revealed through toil in Torah and avodah.
Tamuz is linked to the letter ches, whose first appearance in the Torah is choshech, darkness; Tamuz with its milui equals 'yehi or', so the darkness turns to light.
A child circumcised on Rosh Chodesh Tamuz is suited to toil in Torah and avodah and to reveal the light of Torah and of Klal Yisrael.
Milah is given to an infant because the holiness of a Jew, rooted in Avraham, is above daas; tefillin, by contrast, is the peak of daas.
Jews have two kinds of holiness: what Hashem gives them, and what they work for themselves, represented by milah and tefillin.

title.en: Tamuz: great light covered like the orlah

summary.en: The Rav notes the bris falls on Rosh Chodesh Tamuz, whose fasts the navi says will become festivals. As the holiness of the bris is covered by an orlah, the brightest month is covered, and through toil in Torah and avodah one finds the Shechinah 'bein hametzarim'.

title.en: The letter ches: turning darkness to light

summary.en: The Rav brings Sefer Yetzirah that Tamuz is ruled by the letter ches, the first ches in the Torah being choshech, and shows that Tamuz with its milui equals 'yehi or'. A child circumcised on Rosh Chodesh, which holds the whole month, is suited to reveal the light under the darkness; he blesses the parents.

title.en: Sasson and yekar: milah and tefillin

summary.en: From the Gemara that 'sasson' is milah and 'yekar' is tefillin, the Rav asks why milah is not delayed until the child can do it knowingly, and answers that a Jew's holiness is above daas, while tefillin are the peak of daas. Everyone at a bris should be stirred to bring that root into daas, and he closes with blessings for the geulah.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Behaaloscha, the Rav speaks of the kindling of the menorah and explains that while Eliyahu HaNavi's emissaries come to every bris, at a special bris like this one Eliyahu comes himself.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a theme from Parshas Behaaloscha, the menorah and its daily kindling and preparation, though most of this opening is too garbled to follow. He then turns to the bris itself: Eliyahu HaNavi comes to every bris, but usually it is his emissaries who come, while at a truly special bris Eliyahu comes himself, and he says today's bris is such a one. He speaks of the importance of a bris in a family that has lived through hard times, and closes with blessings that the parents raise the child to Torah and good deeds.

en: The Rav opens with the menorah of Parshas Behaaloscha, its kindling and the preparing of its lamps.
Eliyahu HaNavi comes to every bris, but at most only his emissaries come, while at a very special bris he comes himself.
The Rav says that today's bris is such a bris, to which Eliyahu comes himself.
A bris in a family that has gone through hard times is an especially precious bris.

title.en: The menorah, and Eliyahu at a special bris

summary.en: The Rav opens with the menorah of Behaaloscha, then explains that Eliyahu's emissaries come to every bris but Eliyahu himself comes to a special bris, as he says today's is. He speaks of the worth of a bris in a family that has known hardship and closes with blessings for the child and parents.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Behaaloscha, the Rav explains Rashi's praise that Aharon 'did not change': he chose the lamps, which bring Torah and sons who are talmidei chachamim, over the ketores, which brings wealth, every day for forty years, and wishes that this home merit both together.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Rashi on 'vaya'as ken Aharon' in this week's parsha: it tells Aharon's praise, that he did not change. He explains that in the Beis HaMikdash the one who merited to offer the ketores had a promise of wealth, while the avodah of preparing the lamps brought the merit of Torah and of sons who are talmidei chachamim. Aharon, who could pick any avodah he wished, took the lamps every day, and since one person cannot do both, he gave up the ketores. The Rav asks why, in forty years in the desert, Aharon did not give up the lamps even one day to gain a little wealth, as a father needs to marry off children, and answers that this is his praise: he never changed. He then turns to the bris, where Torah is precious in the family, and blesses the father, the grandparents and the guests that the light of Torah shine from the home, together with greatness.

en: Rashi's words on 'vaya'as ken Aharon', that he did not change, are Aharon's praise for lighting the lamps every day.
The Rav says that offering the ketores carried a promise of wealth, while the avodah of the lamps brought Torah and sons who are talmidei chachamim.
Since one person cannot both prepare the lamps and offer the ketores, Aharon's daily choice of the lamps meant giving up the ketores.
The Rav applies this to the bris: in this family Torah is precious, and he wishes that the light of Torah shine from the home.
