title.en: Aharon chose the lamps over the ketores

summary.en: The Rav explains Rashi's praise of Aharon that he did not change: he took the lamps, which bring Torah and sons who are talmidei chachamim, and gave up the ketores, which brings wealth, every day for forty years. He applies it to the family of the bris and closes with blessings for the father, the grandparents and the guests.

catalogTitle: ביאור על תשובה תתאה. עצה למי שאפילו אהבה שכליות אינו יכול לפועל בעצמו. כי קרוב אליך בדרך קצרה - יותר קלה לחלושי כח ע"י האהבה המתוסרת בלבו.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Tanya chapter 17: why 'the thing is very near to you' is true for every Jew through the mind's rule over the heart, why it does not speak to a true rasha, and how even he returns through the lower teshuvah that raises the fallen Hei.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews the previous chapter: one who cannot turn intellectual love and fear into emotion may serve with the mind alone, since some souls are still 'in the womb'. Chapter 17 now applies these ideas to the verse the Tanya's title page names as its purpose, 'ki karov eilecha'. Our senses seem to deny it, since a complete turning of the heart is rare: love cannot be divided, and one who still craves worldly pleasure does not truly love Hashem. He tells stories of tzaddikim who no longer tasted food. The Gemara's 'yirah is a small thing' applies to Moshe Rabbeinu, and what is asked of everyone is action driven by the mind. Logical love, like a mother's love she does not feel, is within every person's power, because the mind rules the heart by nature, except in the true rasha, whose lost control is a punishment. Such a rasha needs teshuvah first: a broken heart, often aroused from above, the lower teshuvah that raises the fallen Hei, connected to Chanukah.

en: One whose soul cannot produce emotional love and fear may serve Hashem with the understanding of the mind alone; not everyone is required to reach the same level.
Love cannot be divided: one who still pursues worldly pleasure and believes he also loves Hashem fully is deceiving himself.
What 'ki karov' promises every Jew is not a transformed heart but mitzvos done because the mind understands the duty.
A person can think as much as he wants even when he cannot love as much as he wants, so logical love is within everyone's reach.
By nature the mind rules the heart and the limbs, except in a true rasha, who as a punishment for his sins has lost that control.
A true rasha cannot begin serving Hashem without first breaking the barrier of the kelipos through a broken heart; this is the lower teshuvah, which returns the lower Hei of Hashem's Name.

candidateTopics: loss of free choice by the rasha

title.en: Review: serving with the mind alone

summary.en: The Rav reviews the previous chapter: Chochmah and Binah meditating on Hashem's greatness should stir love and fear in the heart, but one who cannot may serve with the mind's understanding alone. Such a soul is still 'in the womb' of Knesses Yisroel and not yet 'born', so revealed love is not required of it.

title.en: Chapter 17 and the verse 'ki karov'

summary.en: The Rav explains that chapter 17 begins a new phase, applying the earlier axioms in practice, and that the title page names the verse 'ki karov eilecha' as the Tanya's purpose. He raises the difficulty that our senses seem to deny it, and rejects the idea that it applied only to Moshe Rabbeinu's generation: the Torah speaks to every generation and every person.

title.en: Love cannot be divided

summary.en: The Rav explains why turning the heart from worldly desire to true love of Hashem is so hard: love is indivisible and can be directed to only one object. With the example of enjoying an ice cream, he says that one who still desires worldly pleasure and thinks he also loves Hashem is imagining it, though thinking of Hashem while eating is better than nothing.

title.en: Tzaddikim beyond the taste of food

summary.en: The Rav says the Ba'al HaTanya and his chassidim experienced this level, and tells of tzaddikim in recent times: one who said he had not known the taste of food for twenty years, two Rebbes recalling the wartime transports, and the Yismach Moshe, who ate dishwater thinking it was soup. He ends that one who still enjoys the ice cream should not fool himself that his love of Hashem is complete.

title.en: 'Yirah is a small thing' for Moshe

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that calls yirah a small thing for Moshe Rabbeinu, and explains that a complete transformation of the heart belongs to tzaddikim like Dovid HaMelech, not to beinonim. What Hashem asks of everyone, as the previous chapters explained, is enough yirah in the mind to drive the doing.

title.en: Doing the mitzvah from the mind's duty

summary.en: The Rav stresses that the Tanya does not say to refrain from the ice cream; it says that when a mitzvah comes, the mind should recognize the duty and act. His example is tefillin: one may not feel the glow, but feels the obligation because Hashem requires it, and this suffices for a soul from ibbur rather than leidah.

title.en: Logical love is in every person's power

summary.en: The Rav explains that the level near to everyone is a logical love, even if it is not revealed in the heart like flames of fire, because the mind is in a person's power: he cannot love as he wishes but can think as he wishes. He compares it to a mother's love that she does not always feel, and says the felt joy of the mitzvah is its reward, granted to tzaddikim but not required of everyone in this world.

title.en: The mind rules the heart, except in a rasha

summary.en: The Rav explains that by nature the mind controls the heart, the mouth and the limbs, except in a true rasha, who has lost that control; he brings Chazal that the wicked are in the power of their heart and the heart of tzaddikim is in their power, and the question of Pharaoh's hardened heart. He explains the loss of control as a punishment that began with free choice, comparing it to a case in the Gemara that starts with negligence and ends with compulsion, and concludes that 'ki karov' does not speak to such reshaim, who are called dead in their lifetime.

title.en: How a rasha begins: a broken heart

summary.en: The Rav asks how one who lost his free choice can do teshuvah, and answers that every Jew has a point that evil cannot touch, which Hashem sometimes arouses through circumstances. A rasha can do a mitzvah here and there, but to begin real service he must first break the iron wall of the kelipos with a broken heart; this is the lower teshuvah, as opposed to the higher teshuvah from love.

title.en: Raising the fallen Hei; Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav explains that sin separates the lower Hei, the Shechinah, from the Name, dragging it into exile with the person, and teshuvah, 'tashuv Hei', returns it. He connects this to Chanukah of the coming month Kislev: the wicks and oils that do not burn on Shabbos burn on Chanukah, since then Hashem comes down to lift the fallen; he ends with the Tanya's description of the rasha's soul in exile.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Parshas Balak, the Rav explains that the parsha is named for the hidden spark of Moshiach in Balak, that the days of bein hametzarim hold great kedusha covered by an orlah, and that a bris now is a sign that Hashem will remove that orlah and bring the geulah.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why a parsha should be named after Balak. He explains that Balak usually falls just before the three weeks, and the holy sefarim say these days will become the greatest days, as Zechariah says the fasts will turn to joy; now they are covered by din. Where kedusha is greatest the kelipah is strongest, as the Sfas Emes says, in a person, in a place such as Eretz Yisrael, and in time. Hashem will come as the mohel and remove this orlah. Balak, a terrible kelipah, held a holy spark, for Chazal say he was the ancestor of Rus and so of Moshiach ben David; the parsha is named for that spark. Balak feared that the orlah would be removed and Moshiach revealed, but in the end the spark came out. A bris in this week is therefore a good sign, and the Rav says that at such a bris Eliyahu HaNavi himself comes, and he blesses the family.

en: The days of bein hametzarim are destined to be the greatest days of the year, but now they are covered by din.
Where kedusha is greatest, the kelipah over it is strongest, and it must be cut away.
The parsha is named after Balak because of the holy spark in him, from which Moshiach ben David descends.
A bris in Parshas Balak is a good sign that Hashem will remove the orlah of these days and reveal their kedusha.
Eliyahu HaNavi, the herald of the geulah, comes to every bris, and to an important bris he comes himself.

title.en: Great kedusha covered by an orlah

summary.en: The Rav asks why a parsha is named after Balak, and explains that the coming days of bein hametzarim hold the greatest kedusha, now covered by din, because where kedusha is greatest the kelipah is strongest, in a person, a place and a time. Hashem will come as the mohel and remove the orlah.

title.en: Balak's hidden spark and the bris

summary.en: The Rav explains that Balak held a spark of Moshiach, as the ancestor of Rus, and feared its revelation, yet it came out in the end; a bris in this week is a good sign of the geulah. He adds that Eliyahu HaNavi himself comes to an important bris and closes with blessings for the family.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the nine days, the Rav explains that the bris removes the orlah that covers kedusha, in a person, in a place and in time, and that the mourning set aside for a bris in these days is a sign that Hashem will remove the orlah of churban and reveal their greatness.

abstract.en: The Rav asks what connection a bris has to the customs of the nine days, which are set aside for it: the participants may eat meat, drink wine and take a haircut. He explains that a bris removes the orlah from the holy covenant and reveals the kedusha of the Jewish child, and that, following Sefer Yetzirah, there is orlah in a person, in a place and in time. Eretz Yisrael and Yerushalayim, the place of the Mikdash and the Shechinah, are now covered by an orlah made by the galus, which Moshiach will remove. These days too, which the holy sefarim call great days and which Zechariah says will turn to joy, are covered by the orlah of churban. A bris in the nine days, when the mourning is lifted, is therefore a sign that the orlah of the time will be removed, and he blesses that Eliyahu HaNavi come and bring the geulah.

en: The bris sets aside the mourning customs of the nine days: meat, wine and haircuts are permitted to those taking part.
A bris removes the orlah and reveals the kedusha that is covered in a Jewish child.
Orlah exists in three dimensions, in a person, in a place and in time.
Eretz Yisrael, the place of the Mikdash, is now covered by an orlah made by the galus, which Moshiach will remove to reveal the Shechinah.
The days of the three weeks are destined to be great days, but are now covered by the orlah of churban.

bein hametzarim as days of future joy

title.en: Orlah over a child and over the land

summary.en: The Rav asks why a bris sets aside the customs of the nine days, and explains that a bris removes the orlah from a child's kedusha. Orlah exists in a person, a place and time; Eretz Yisrael, the place of the Mikdash, is now covered by the orlah of galus.

title.en: The orlah of the time and the bris

summary.en: The Rav explains that these days are destined to be great days, as Zechariah says, but are covered by the orlah of churban; a bris now, when the mourning is lifted, is a sign that Hashem will remove that orlah. He closes with blessings that Eliyahu HaNavi come and bring the geulah.

catalogTitle: ביאור חכמה ובינה. חכמה - שורש מחשבתו - י"ח כח מה. צריך להיות פתי בענין אמונה.

oneLiner.en: Opening Tanya chapter 18, the Rav explains the 'short way' for small minds: the hidden love and emunah every Jew inherits from the Avos, rooted in the chochmah at the core of the soul that is bound to the Or Ein Sof.

abstract.en: The Rav first completes the previous chapter: a ba'al teshuvah, having sunk into the depths of tumah, raises sparks of kedushah no tzaddik can reach, and he illustrates it with the story of the Bach in Gehinnom. Turning to chapter 18, he reviews the 'long way' of contemplation through chochmah and binah and introduces the 'short way' for small souls who cannot dwell on Hashem's greatness. Every Jew has a hidden love and natural emunah, an inheritance from the Avos, who are true fathers. A Jew who denies Hashem is like a sick stomach that has lost its appetite. The Avos were a merkavah for Hashem and passed this to all their descendants, down to the lowest soul, whose inner core is chochmah, bound to the Or Ein Sof, because souls are not created yesh me'ayin. From the Sefer HaGilgulim he explains how a rasha can beget a tzaddik, and how Moshiach's lineage was hidden in klippah from the Satan.

en: Tanya chapter 18 begins a 'short way' for people whose minds cannot dwell long on Hashem's greatness, after the 'long way' of chochmah and binah in the earlier chapters.
Every Jew has a hidden love and a natural emunah in Hashem, an inheritance from the Avos rather than something acquired.
Because the Avos were a merkavah for Hashem, they passed His powers on to all their descendants, even to the lowest soul of nefesh de'nefesh of Malchus de'Asiyah.
Hidden in every soul is chochmah, its inner core, in which the Or Ein Sof is clothed.
Jewish souls, unlike the rest of creation, are not made yesh me'ayin but are a direct extension from Hashem, like children.
Since even a rasha's inner core is bound to the Ein Sof, a rasha can sometimes beget a tzaddik far greater than himself.

candidateTopics: hidden love of the Jewish soul
emunah as an inheritance from the Avos
chochmah as the core of the soul
teshuvah and raising sparks of kedushah
a rasha who begets a tzaddik

title.en: The ba'al teshuvah raises lost sparks

summary.en: Completing the previous chapter, the Rav explains that sparks of kedushah scattered by Adam's sin are raised when used for good, that the higher the kedushah the deeper it sank, and that a rasha who does teshuvah lifts sparks no tzaddik can reach.

title.en: The Bach in Gehinnom

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Bach, found without sin, had to pass briefly through Gehinnom because a sneeze moved a wagon drawn by an ox and a horse, and there he decreed that its fire be put out for forty days, raising the resha'im with him.

title.en: From the long way to the short way

summary.en: Opening chapter 18, the Rav reviews the earlier chapters: love and fear born of chochmah and binah, or at least a mind that understands. He then introduces the chapters for small souls who cannot harness their minds, and the Tanya's reminder that one would give his life rather than serve avodah zarah, as the 'short way' promised on the title page.

title.en: 'Very near': a third way

summary.en: The Rav reads the opening of chapter 18 on the passuk 'very near to you': even one who cannot meditate on Hashem's greatness nor understand it with his mind has a third way, emunah, and the love in his heart is real, not imagined.

title.en: An inheritance from the Avos

summary.en: The Rav explains that the hidden love is an inheritance from the Avos, called fathers and not grandfathers because their closeness never fades. Every Jew believes; one who denies is like a man who spoiled his stomach and lost his appetite, while the craving is still there.

title.en: The Avos as a merkavah

summary.en: Asking what the root of this love is, the Rav explains that the Avos were a merkavah for Hashem, like the chariot Yechezkel saw, never separated from Him for a moment, and so they passed all the G-dly powers of the ten sefiros to every descendant, even to the poshei Yisrael.

title.en: Chochmah at the core of every soul

summary.en: The Rav describes the levels of souls, from Atzilus down to nefesh de'nefesh of Malchus de'Asiyah, and explains that since the sefiros are bound into one, even the lowest soul contains chochmah, its inner kernel, in which the Or Ein Sof rests, as the pesukim say Hashem founded the world with chochmah.

title.en: Not yesh me'ayin but a direct extension

summary.en: The Rav explains that all creation comes from Hashem as beriah, something from nothing, but a Jewish soul is a direct extension from Him, like a child. Like life that fills every limb of the body, this G-dly chochmah gives life to every Jew, high or low.

title.en: A rasha who begets a tzaddik

summary.en: From the Arizal's Sefer HaGilgulim the Rav asks how a rasha can beget a tzaddik if each creature begets its own kind, and answers that the rasha's inner core is bound to the Ein Sof. He then explains that Yaakov and Esav were born together so that the Samach Mem would have no complaint about the balance of good and evil.

title.en: Two kinds of admoni

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Esav the admoni, a shedder of blood drawn to red, with David, an admoni with beautiful eyes whose bloodshed was with the Sanhedrin's permission, and mentions the custom not to wear red. He then brings the Midrash that the Satan guarded against Moshiach's birth, and so it came hidden, as with Moav, whom the Satan never suspected.

title.en: Great souls hidden in klippah

summary.en: The Rav continues with Rus and David, whom the Satan took for his own, and with the Arizal's account of Avraham's birth, concluding that a rasha can draw down a holy soul hidden in klippah because even he holds chochmah bound to the Ein Sof. Answering a question at the end, he distinguishes a middah, which habit can change, from an existing entity such as the love of Hashem in every Jew.

oneLiner.en: At a bris seudah, the Rav explains that while every generation, year and moment has its own task, the bris is the eternal covenant that carries Yiddishkeit and emunah unchanged from one generation to the next.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with 'to pass into the covenant' from Parshas Nitzavim and explains that a bris is something made eternal. He brings Rashi in Parshas Noach that a covenant was needed so the fruits would not spoil. Every generation, year and moment has its own conduct and task, to be fulfilled in its time, yet beneath the change runs the eternity of Klal Yisroel: to be Hashem's chosen people, do His will and crown Him King over the world. Names change with each mission, as Rashi says, but this never changes. Milah, unlike other mitzvos, hands emunah from one generation to the next, a covenant made even with the unborn. Amalek, who scorned milah, fights this eternity, so Hashem's war with him lasts from generation to generation. The Rav closes with blessings.

en: A bris is something made eternal: like the covenant over the fruits in Noach's ark, it is what keeps a thing from spoiling.
Every generation, year and moment has its own conduct and its own task that must be fulfilled at that time.
Beneath every change there is an eternity of Klal Yisroel that never changes, and this is the meaning of the bris.
The Jewish people's task, to be Hashem's chosen people, do His will and crown Him King over the whole world, does not change from day to day, year to year or generation to generation.
Milah differs from other mitzvos: it is the handing down of emunah and Yiddishkeit from one generation to the next.
Amalek, who scorned milah, is the force that opposes the eternity of Klal Yisroel, and so Hashem's war with him is from generation to generation.

title.en: The bris as what makes things eternal

summary.en: The Rav opens with 'to pass into the covenant' from Parshas Nitzavim and Rashi in Parshas Noach on the covenant over the fruits, and explains that a bris preserves. He contrasts this with the changing conduct of every generation, year and moment, beneath which runs the eternity of Klal Yisroel.

title.en: Milah: handing emunah to the next generation

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Jewish people's role toward Hashem never changes, though names change with each mission, and that milah, unlike other mitzvos, carries emunah from generation to generation, a covenant made even with the unborn. He then explains Amalek, who scorned milah, as the force opposing this eternity, hence the war 'from generation to generation'.

title.en: The father's mesirus nefesh and blessings

summary.en: The Rav praises the father's mesirus nefesh for emunah and Yiddishkeit, says this gives an assurance that Amalek will have no hold here, and that today's bris is made with the generations to come. He closes with blessings that Yiddishkeit continue in the family and that Hashem's kingship be revealed over the whole world.

oneLiner.en: At a bris, the Rav explains why the Harachaman for Moshiach mentions the 'chasan damim' of Moshe Rabbeinu's son, and why a bris in a time of weakened milah is a harbinger of the geulah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Harachaman prayers said at a bris and asks why the one for Moshiach is tied to the merit of 'chasan damim lamulos', the milah of Moshe Rabbeinu's son, and why it speaks of good tidings. He asks how Moshe Rabbeinu could have delayed his son's milah, and compares it to the Midrash on the breaking of the luchos: Moshe did not want to be separated from klal Yisroel. Using the Ibn Ezra that milah is a sign by which Jews recognize one another, he explains that the punishment of kareis for not doing milah, like that for eating on Yom Kippur, comes from cutting oneself off from the community. In Egypt the Jews had stopped doing milah, and Moshe, pained by this, held back his own son's milah to arouse mercy above for all of them. Today too milah has been weakened among millions of Jews, so a bris now is a sign that the geulah is near. He closes with blessings for the family.

en: The Rav asks why the Harachaman for Moshiach is said in the merit of 'chasan damim lamulos', when Moshiach should come in his own merit.
Following the Ibn Ezra, the Rav says milah is a sign by which Jews everywhere recognize one another as Jews.
The kareis for not doing milah, like the kareis for eating on Yom Kippur, is explained as the result of separating oneself from klal Yisroel.
Moshe Rabbeinu held back his son's milah because the Jews in Egypt were not circumcising, in order to arouse mercy above for them.
In our time, as before the Exodus, milah has been weakened among millions of Jews, so a bris now is a good sign that the geulah is coming.

kareis and separation from the community

title.en: Harachaman, Moshiach and 'chasan damim'

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Harachaman for Moshiach at a bris mentions the merit of 'chasan damim lamulos' and good tidings. He then asks how Moshe Rabbeinu could have delayed his son's milah, and points to the Midrash that Moshe broke the luchos because he did not want to be separate from klal Yisroel.

title.en: Milah as the sign of belonging to klal Yisroel

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ibn Ezra that milah is a sign by which Jews recognize each other, and a sefer's explanation that kareis for eating on Yom Kippur comes from separating from the community; the same applies to milah. Since in Egypt the Jews had stopped doing milah, Moshe Rabbeinu held back his own son's milah to arouse mercy above, which is why it says 'lamulos' in the plural.

title.en: A bris today as a harbinger of the geulah

summary.en: The Rav compares our time, before the geulah, to the time before the Exodus: milah has been weakened among millions of Jews in Russia, America and everywhere. Since Moshe Rabbeinu is connected to Moshiach, a bris in the week of the parsha of bris milah is a good sign of redemption; he ends with blessings for the father, the family and all present.

oneLiner.en: At a bris, the Rav links the father's eight days of involvement in his son's milah to the Jew whose heart is always in Yerushalayim, and blesses him to merit seeing the Shechinah three times a year.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Harachaman of the bris that links the milah on the eighth day to going up to see the Shechinah three times a year. He explains that a Jew longs all year for the time he can go to Yerushalayim for Yom Tov, and as the passuk says of the Beis HaMikdash, 'My eyes and My heart shall be there all the days': since his thoughts are there, it is as if he is there constantly. He then brings Tosafos' question why a passuk is needed to exempt a woman from milah, and an answer in the Rishonim: the father is bound by the mitzvah day and night for all eight days, since he must arrange that the bris be on time. Today, when problems with a bris on the eighth day are common and a father runs between doctor and rav, he is busy with the mitzvah all eight days; measure for measure, the Rav blesses him to go up to Yerushalayim and see the Shechinah.

en: A Jew who longs all year for Yerushalayim has his heart there constantly, so it is as if he is always there.
According to an answer in the Rishonim, milah is not a time-bound mitzvah for the father, since he is obligated day and night for all eight days to make sure the bris happens on time.

When a father runs between doctor and rav for eight days and nights to arrange the bris, he is busy with the mitzvah the whole time, and measure for measure should merit going up to see the Shechinah.

title.en: Eight days of milah and the longing for Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Rav connects the Harachaman's blessing to see the Shechinah three times a year with the eight days of milah. He explains that a Jew whose heart is always in Yerushalayim is as if there constantly, brings an answer in the Rishonim that the father is bound by the mitzvah all eight days, and applies it to a father who ran between doctor and rav to arrange the bris.

catalogTitle: טבע נשמות ישראל להיות בטל להקב"ה לגמרי י"ט כדי להתאחד באור אין סוף ב"ה וב"ש.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Tanya chapter 18: because Hashem is clothed in the Chochmah of every Jewish soul, even the simplest Jew has an instinctive emunah, above reason, that makes him ready to give his life rather than deny Hashem's unity.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by recalling the levels of the previous chapter and asks how the verse 'it is very close to you' applies to a Jew who cannot even intellectually grasp Hashem's greatness. The answer begins with the Avos, whose qualities their children inherit. He then explains Chochmah as the fountain of intellect: the sudden spark, above the mind, that Binah develops, compared to the tefillin above the brain. Since no thought can grasp Hashem, emunah is above reason, like a child's knowledge of his parents. He brings the Chasam Sofer's ruling that a son may not kill his father who breaks in, because a father's bond to his son is instinctive. With 'a simple one believes everything', 'I was like a beast with You' and 'an ox knows its owner', he shows that this emunah is instinct. Hence even the lowest Jews gave their lives, unlike drilled soldiers, and nearly all keep milah and avoid chametz.

en: Chochmah is the source of intellect: a spark from above that the mind receives but cannot grasp, which Binah then develops into understanding.
Emunah is above reason; in emunah everyone is like a simple fool, and the greatest wisdom in emunah is simple faith.
A Jew knows Hashem by intuition, the way a child knows his father and mother without being able to explain why.
Even the lowest Jews gave their lives rather than deny Hashem's unity, not out of thought or drilling, but by an instinct like a mother animal protecting its young.
Idolatry is like suicide for the neshamah, so a Jew instinctively gives up his body to save it, as a hand reflexively shields the eye.

summary.en: The Rav reviews the levels of the previous chapter and asks how the verse 'it is very close to you' applies to a Jew who cannot even intellectually grasp Hashem's greatness. He explains that the Avos were a merkavah, and their children inherit their qualities, revealed or hidden.

title.en: Chochmah, the fountain of intellect

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chochmah is not wisdom but the source of the sudden spark of insight that Binah develops. He compares it to tefillin, which sit above the brain, brings Pasach Eliyahu, and reads Chochmah as 'koach mah', a power we cannot grasp.

title.en: Pure logic and emunah above reason

summary.en: The Rav says no thought can grasp Hashem, discusses the Gemara that women have extra Binah yet rarely pure logic, and adds that most men's thinking is also biased by desire. Emunah is above reason, like a child who knows his parents without understanding why.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer on a father and son

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer's ruling that a son may not kill his father who breaks in, even if the father does not recognize him, because a father instinctively will not kill his son. With Reb Chaim Brisker's remark on the Rosh, he explains that a ruling without proof comes from a mind molded by Torah.

title.en: The simple one, the beast and the ox

summary.en: The Rav reads 'a simple one believes everything' and says the greatest wisdom in emunah is simplicity. He explains 'I was like a beast with You' and 'an ox knows its owner': an animal knows its master by instinct, and so does a Jew.

title.en: Self-sacrifice by instinct, not by thought

summary.en: The Rav explains that even the lowest Jews endure torture rather than deny Hashem without thinking it through, like a mother animal defending its young. He contrasts this with soldiers who were trained to give their lives for the king.

title.en: The chassid and the flogged soldier

summary.en: The Rav tells of a chassid who came to the Ba'al HaTanya after years away; he had seen a soldier flogged for coming back from guard duty with frozen ears, and that stirred his davening for years. He explains that today there is no fear of the king, and describes how soldiers were drilled until they would die for the king.

title.en: Undrilled Jews who gave their lives

summary.en: The Rav notes that no Jew would blow himself up for a political leader, yet history shows sinful Jews who let themselves be killed in the Crusades rather than convert. He adds that one who says Shema with intent and readies himself for mesirus nefesh, as the Zohar says, has worked himself up to it.

title.en: Exceptions, and milah and chametz

summary.en: The Rav brings the Tzemach Tzedek that sins connected with gentiles, such as chalav akum, yayin nesech or chametz on Pesach, deaden the feeling for mesirus nefesh. He mentions a survey in Eretz Yisrael that nearly everyone keeps milah and avoids chametz, and explains that Hashem Echad lights up the whole soul through Chochmah.

title.en: Milah above reason; idolatry as suicide of the soul

summary.en: The Rav brings the dispute of Yishmael and Yitzchak over milah and explains that milah is above daas, in a Jew's blood. Idolatry is suicide for the neshamah, so a Jew instinctively sacrifices the body for it, like a hand shielding the eye; he closes with a remark on Greek culture.

oneLiner.en: At a bris, the Rav explains that milah, Avraham Avinu's inheritance of emunah, is above daas, and that this bris joins that emunah with the daas of a family of Torah, like sasson (milah) together with yekar (tefillin).

abstract.en: The Rav opens by tying milah specifically to Avraham Avinu, the first of the believers, who left all Jewish children an inheritance of emunah. Emunah, he explains, is higher than daas, and the root of Klal Yisroel cannot be grasped by the mind. That is why milah is given to an eight-day-old infant who has no daas yet: one might ask why not wait until the child understands, but milah is entirely a matter of emunah above daas. He adds that even Jews who keep nothing else still keep milah, because a person can choose to be a tzaddik or a rasha but not whether to be a Jew. Turning to this bris, he cites Chazal that sasson is milah and yekar is tefillin: milah is wholly above daas, tefillin is the peak of daas, and this family, distinguished in Torah and yiras shamayim, joins the two. He ends with blessings for the child.

en: Milah is bound to Avraham Avinu, who left all Jewish children an inheritance of emunah.
Emunah is above daas, and the root of Klal Yisroel cannot be grasped by the mind.
Milah is given to an infant without daas, because it is entirely a matter of emunah above daas.
Even Jews who keep no other mitzvah keep milah, since being a Jew is beyond a person's free choice.
Sasson is milah, above daas; yekar is tefillin, the peak of daas; this bris joins the two.

title.en: Milah: Avraham's emunah above daas

summary.en: The Rav ties milah to Avraham Avinu, the first believer, who left Jewish children an inheritance of emunah, which is above daas. He asks why milah is not delayed until the child has understanding, and answers that milah, like emunah, is above daas.

title.en: Sasson and yekar: milah with tefillin

summary.en: The Rav notes that even non-observant Jews keep milah, because being a Jew is beyond choice. He then brings Chazal that sasson is milah and yekar is tefillin, says this family of Torah joins emunah above daas with the peak of daas, and blesses the child.

oneLiner.en: At a bris held minutes before sunset in the week of parshas Shemos, the Rav explains that milah is bound up with the geulah, and that a bris that cannot be pushed off any later should arouse Heaven that the geulah cannot wait.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Chazal that Moshe Rabbeinu was born circumcised and asks: milah exists to cut away the bad, and the Chinuch says man was created incomplete so that he should perfect himself, so why was Moshe born already circumcised? He answers that milah, the eighth, belongs to the days of Moshiach, and Moshe is the first and final redeemer. Following the Maharal, a redeemer must stand outside what he redeems, so Moshe, who will remove idolatry from the world, had to be a 'mohel' from birth, and Dovid too was born circumcised as the soul of Moshiach. He then brings Avraham Avinu's zerizus and the custom to do a bris early in the morning, since milah is a plea for the geulah to come quickly. This bris, delayed until minutes before sunset, he reads as a sign that the geulah cannot wait, and he blesses the child, named after two tzaddikim.

en: Moshe Rabbeinu was born circumcised, which seems to contradict the purpose of milah as a person's own perfection.
Milah, the eighth, is connected to the days of Moshiach, and Moshe is both the first and the final redeemer.
A redeemer must be outside what he redeems, so Moshe and Dovid, the redeemers, were born circumcised.
A bris is done early in the morning out of zerizus, following Avraham Avinu, because milah is a plea for a speedy geulah.
A bris pushed to the last minutes before sunset signals that the geulah too can no longer be delayed.

title.en: Why Moshe was born circumcised

summary.en: The Rav asks why Moshe was born circumcised when milah is meant for a person to perfect himself. He answers that milah belongs to Moshiach, that Moshe is the first and final redeemer, and that, per the Maharal, a redeemer must stand outside the impurity he removes, as Dovid too was born circumcised.

title.en: A bris at sunset: the geulah cannot wait

summary.en: The Rav brings Avraham Avinu's zerizus and the custom of an early-morning bris as a plea for a quick geulah. He then reads this bris, held minutes before sunset in the week of parshas Shemos, as a sign that the geulah cannot be delayed, and blesses the child named after two tzaddikim.

catalogTitle: האדם צריך לעשות חשבון שהרי כדי שלא לעבוד ע"ז הי' מוסר נפשו' וכל עבירה הוי מרידה בהקב"ה והוי ממש כמו ע"ז.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's image of the soul as 'the candle of Hashem': like a flame that surges upward to its source even at the cost of its own existence, the Jewish soul by nature longs to be nullified in Hashem, the way of kedushah, while tumah clings to its own ego.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by recalling the previous chapter: even simple Jews steeped in sin are ready to give their lives rather than serve idols, and the coming chapters explain why. He introduces the verse 'the soul of man is the candle of Hashem', and expands with a thought on Chanukah as a glimpse of the light of Moshiach, illustrated by a story of the Chozeh of Lublin. Returning to the Tanya, he describes how a flame surges upward to rejoin its root in the sphere of the moon, why it flickers from side to side, and why Jews sway when they learn. Unlike every other being, fire is ready to be extinguished to return to its source; the soul likewise longs to be nullified in Hashem. He explains that 'nature' means what reason cannot explain, then contrasts kedushah, rooted in Chochmah and bittul, with tumah, which is ego. This leads to true humility, the selfish 'giver' of kelipah called Kna'ani, and the tzaddik whose body alone holds his soul back.

en: The soul is 'the candle of Hashem': like a flame, which always surges upward to rejoin its root, the soul by nature longs to leave and cleave to its source, Hashem.
Fire is the exception in creation: every other being fights to preserve its existence, yet fire is ready to be extinguished as long as it returns to its root, and the soul is the same.
The word 'nature' is a borrowed term for whatever cannot be explained by reason; the soul's urge to cleave to Hashem is 'nature' in this sense, higher than logic, because it comes from Chochmah.
Kedushah means bittul, being ready to be nullified to Hashem, while tumah is ego: it insists on its own separate existence.
True humility is not feeling inferior but having no sense of self apart from Hashem; such an anav is always joyful, while one who is depressed over his shortcomings is really showing pride.
In kedushah the giving side is stronger than the receiving side; in the sitra achra the 'giver' really gives for himself, and that is why it is called Kna'ani, from the word for submitting.
The tzaddik surges toward Hashem without concern for his own existence; only his body, the 'wick', holds his soul back until his time comes.

title.en: Why sinners give their lives; the candle of Hashem

summary.en: The Rav recalls that even sinners are ready for mesiras nefesh against idolatry and says the coming chapters explain why. He introduces 'the soul of man is the candle of Hashem' and brings the teaching that wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos are fit for Chanukah, applied to souls that Shabbos does not ignite but Chanukah does.

title.en: Chanukah, light of Moshiach, and the Chozeh's story

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah's eight lights reach beyond Shabbos's seven into the light of Moshiach, so it can stir even distant souls; when a Jew lights below, Hashem lights his soul above. He tells the story of the Chozeh of Lublin, who would not curse an informer at the moment he was lighting Chanukah candles.

title.en: Why a flame surges upward

summary.en: Back in the Tanya, the Rav explains that a flame always stands upright because it wants to tear loose from the wick and rejoin the general element of fire, whose root is in the sphere of the moon. He describes the invisible spheres and the Rambam's statement that they are pure like clear glass, and the rule that every being yearns for its origin.

title.en: Bedikas chametz at night; why Jews sway

summary.en: The Rav uses the flame's root in the moon to explain why a candle works better at night, hence bedikas chametz at night. The flame shakes side to side like a tooth being pulled, and so Jews sway when they learn or daven; he tells of two babies mixed up at birth, where the one who swayed over Gemara was the Jew.

title.en: Fire and soul ready for self-nullification

summary.en: The Rav explains that the flame strives to free itself even though it would then be extinguished, against the rule that every being fights to preserve itself. The soul, including its lower levels of ruach and nefesh, acts likewise: it longs to cleave to Hashem, the source of all life, even if it would cease to exist as itself.

title.en: What 'nature' means: beyond explanation

summary.en: The Rav explains that the word 'nature' is a borrowed term for what has no reason. He brings the Rashab's point that a scientist can say a hard, sharp knife cuts soft challah but not why, and the example of a machine whose workings can be explained only down to a point; the soul's urge to cleave to Hashem is 'nature' in this sense.

title.en: Kedushah is bittul, tumah is ego; true humility

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chochmah is the potential that produces logic and is higher than it. In kedushah there is an urge to be nullified to Hashem, while tumah is ego, the 'capital I'. He then defines true humility as having no self apart from Hashem, shows how Dovid HaMelech could demand honor without ego, and says a true anav is always joyful.

title.en: Kelipah acts for itself; right over left

summary.en: The Rav explains that whoever draws from Chochmah is nullified and lacks nothing, while kelipah does everything for itself, even its mitzvos. He interprets Chochmah as 'koach mah', the power of nothingness, and lists the seven middos of kelipah, such as its self-praise. In kedushah the giving, right side of chesed dominates, as seen in tefillin, washing and dressing the right side first.

title.en: In kelipah the receiver rules: Kna'ani

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ohr HaChaim's account of his struggle with two dogs, male and female, where the female was far harder to overcome, because in the sitra achra the receiving side is stronger. He applies this to the nations' 'ladies first' and to Rashi's contrast of Yaakov and Esav, and explains that chesed of kelipah is called Kna'ani because its 'giver' really gives for himself.

title.en: The merchant, the tzaddik, and the word 'me'

summary.en: The Rav explains why a merchant is called Kna'ani, then contrasts the tzaddik who gives out of pure chesed and surges to Hashem, held back only by his body, the wick. He brings Nadav and Avihu and Sarah Imeinu as souls that flew out from closeness to Hashem, and closes with a story of a son who learned nothing if he can still say 'me'.

oneLiner.en: At the bris of a boy named Dovid, the Rav explains Chazal that Dovid HaMelech was born circumcised: born of a refined lineage, he had no waste to remove, and the name Dovid points to purity and temimus.

abstract.en: The Rav notes that the child is named Dovid after a relative who was no ordinary Jew, a man of mesirus nefesh and Yiddishkeit, as his children and grandchildren show. He brings the Gemara that Dovid HaMelech was born circumcised, reading 'michtam l'Dovid' as 'his wound was whole'. A child, he says, has a connection to the first bearer of his name, as a child named Avraham connects to Avraham's yiras shamayim. Milah normally cuts away the waste in a child, but Dovid, descended from Yehudah, Peretz, Nachshon, Boaz and Yishai, was born refined, with no waste needing removal. A child named Dovid, from a family of Torah, yiras shamayim and chessed on all sides, carries that purity and temimus, and the Rav blesses him to grow to Torah, chuppah and good deeds.

en: The child is named Dovid after a relative of mesirus nefesh and Yiddishkeit, visible in his descendants.
Chazal teach from 'michtam l'Dovid' that Dovid HaMelech was born circumcised.
A child bearing a name has a connection to the first bearer of that name.
Milah cuts away the waste in a child, but Dovid, from a refined lineage, had none to remove.

title.en: The name Dovid and a pure bris

summary.en: The Rav praises the relative the child Dovid is named after, brings Chazal that Dovid HaMelech was born circumcised, and explains that his refined lineage left no waste for milah to remove. He ties the name Dovid to purity and temimus and blesses the child.

oneLiner.en: At a bris, the Rav ties milah to Yom Kippur and the days of Sefirah, and explains that the father who brings his son into the covenant draws upon himself the soul of Avraham Avinu, and that the name is given at the milah because milah leaves a lasting remembrance.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the weeks of Acharei and Kedoshim and says that Yom Kippur is, in its essence, the matter of milah: the Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer says Avraham's bris was on Yom Kippur, and the passuk 'Hashem will circumcise your heart' joins the two. He connects a Masorah mnemonic for the Yom Kippur parsha to the sefirah of yesod, which is milah, as the Zohar says. He then tells what Rabbi Chaim Vital wrote: the Arizal stood up for him because, while busy with redeeming captives, he carried the soul of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair. So too a father who brings his child into the bris of Avraham receives Avraham's soul that day, the trait of chessed. He notes the auspicious time and the child's name, Yaakov Yosef, and blesses the family. In a second part he explains, from Amalek's scorn for milah and his punishment of having his remembrance erased, why the name is given at the milah.

en: The Rav says Yom Kippur is in essence the matter of milah, since Avraham Avinu's bris was on Yom Kippur.
He links the sefirah of yesod to the mitzvah of milah and finds a hint to milah in the Masorah of the Yom Kippur parsha.
A person busy with a mitzvah that a tzaddik was connected to receives that tzaddik's soul; so a father bringing his son into the bris receives the soul of Avraham Avinu that day.
Amalek scorned milah and was punished measure for measure by having his remembrance erased; milah, by contrast, leaves a remembrance, which is why the name is given at the milah.

title.en: Yom Kippur as the matter of milah

summary.en: The Rav says that Yom Kippur, read in Parshas Acharei, is in essence the matter of milah, citing the Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer that Avraham's bris was on Yom Kippur and the passuk of circumcising the heart. He ties a Masorah mnemonic for that parsha to the sefirah of yesod, which is milah.

title.en: Receiving Avraham Avinu's soul at the bris

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Arizal stood up for Rabbi Chaim Vital because, busy with redeeming captives, he carried the soul of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, and applies it: a father bringing his son into the bris receives the soul of Avraham Avinu. He speaks of the auspicious time of Sefirah and the name Yaakov Yosef, and blesses the family.

title.en: Why the name is given at the milah

summary.en: The Rav brings that Amalek scorned milah and was punished measure for measure with the erasing of his remembrance, and explains that milah leaves a lasting remembrance, which is why the child's name is given at the milah. He closes with a blessing for the child.

oneLiner.en: At a pidyon haben, the Rav contrasts Esav's meal that despised the birthright with the pidyon haben meal that honors the firstborn, Hashem who is First, and the Torah called 'reishis', and explains why eating at it is likened to eighty-four fasts.

abstract.en: The Rav says pidyon haben comes from the Exodus, when Hashem said 'sanctify to Me every firstborn', and that on the night of the plague of the firstborn Jews reached a conduct above intellect and time, tied to 'Bereishis', the first utterance. He relates a sefer's account of a Nittel night and says that at a pidyon haben meal such forces have no hold. From 'My firstborn son is Israel' he turns to Esav's meal, where he despised the birthright, and asks why that is stressed when Esav did worse that day. Using Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen's reading of the Rambam on techiyas hameisim, he answers that despising the birthright revealed denial of 'reishis'. The pidyon haben meal is the reverse: it honors the firstborn and the Torah. He explains the saying that such a meal equals eighty-four fasts, notes how Maseches Pesachim ends, and blesses the family.

en: Pidyon haben comes from the Exodus, when on the night of the plague of the firstborn Jews reached a conduct above intellect and above time.
Relative to the angels, the Rav says, Jews are Hashem's firstborn; the verse does not mean that the nations are ordinary sons.
Esav's despising the birthright was singled out because it revealed that he denied 'reishis', the firstness through which Israel and the Torah are bound to Hashem.
The pidyon haben meal is the reverse of Esav's meal: it honors the birthright and the Torah and gives thanks to Hashem.
Eating at a pidyon haben meal is likened to eighty-four fasts, because honoring 'reishis' repairs the root blemish of the first not being given to Hashem.

title.en: Pidyon haben and the night of the Exodus

summary.en: Asked by the father to speak, the Rav says pidyon haben stems from 'sanctify to Me every firstborn' at the Exodus, when Jews reached a conduct above intellect and time. He relates a sefer's account of a Nittel night and says that at a pidyon haben meal such forces have no hold, as on the night when 'no dog sharpened its tongue'.

title.en: Esav's meal and the pidyon haben meal

summary.en: From 'My firstborn son is Israel' the Rav turns to Esav's meal at which he despised the birthright, and asks why this is stressed when Esav did worse that day. Through Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen's reading of the Rambam on techiyas hameisim he answers that it revealed denial of 'reishis', and calls the pidyon haben meal its reverse, a meal honoring the birthright and the Torah.

title.en: A meal equal to eighty-four fasts

summary.en: The Rav brings from the seforim that eating at a pidyon haben meal is like the eighty-four fasts the Arizal gave for a blemish of the bris, and explains that the root blemish is the first not going to Hashem, so honoring 'reishis' repairs it. He notes that Maseches Pesachim ends with the father's blessing, and blesses the family and all of Israel with redemption.

catalogTitle: המשך ביאור לבטל הטענות כנגד מי שאומרים כ"ב שאין כל עבירה כע"ז ממש' מצוה ועבירה הם נצחיות.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 25, the Rav explains why every aveirah is really like avodah zarah, why the hidden love of every Jew makes overcoming the yetzer hara near and easy, and why the claim 'I can do teshuvah later' fails, since a mitzvah and an aveirah are stamped into eternity.

abstract.en: The Rav announces that he will now go to the essence of Tanya, which speaks even to plain people of a very low generation like ours. He recalls that all mitzvos branch out of 'Anochi' and 'Lo yihyeh', and that every Jew, even the simplest, instinctively gives his life rather than worship avodah zarah. Since every aveirah places a person under the sitra achra, it is a hidden form of avodah zarah; sinning anyway is the 'ruach shtus' Chazal learn from the sotah. In chapter 25 he distinguishes faulty reasoning from plain forgetting, and teaches that the remedy is to arouse the hidden love, illustrated by the Avnei Nezer's explanation about a kohenes. The love includes fear, like a mother holding her baby. He answers the argument of later teshuvah: above time nothing is temporary, so an aveirah is eternal. The same applies to positive mitzvos, and he closes with the darkness of the Shovevim weeks.

en: Every Jew, even the simplest, is instinctively ready to give his life rather than worship avodah zarah, without being trained for it.
Any aveirah, even a small rabbinic one, places a person under the jurisdiction of the sitra achra and is a subdivision of avodah zarah.
One sins either out of 'shtus', faulty reasoning, or out of 'shikchah', simply not thinking; the remedy is to remember and arouse the hidden love for Hashem.
The hidden love includes fear: one fears damaging the love, and it works as a G-dly instinct beyond reasoning.
The plea 'I will do teshuvah afterwards' fails, since a Jew would not worship avodah zarah even temporarily although teshuvah would help there too.
Above, there is no time, so an aveirah is not temporary; it is stamped into eternity, and the soul senses this.
The same reckoning applies to positive mitzvos: one must fight laziness, which comes from the element of earth, in Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.

candidateTopics: teshuvah and 'I will sin and repent'

title.en: Going to the essence of Tanya

summary.en: The Rav says he will skip ahead to the core chapters of Tanya, which speak to plain people. He describes our generation as very low, with the signs Chazal give for the time before Moshiach, and says even so people like us can benefit from these chapters.

title.en: Mesirus nefesh for avodah zarah

summary.en: The Rav recalls that all mitzvos branch out of 'Anochi' and 'Lo yihyeh', and that every Jew, even the simplest, gives his life rather than serve avodah zarah, unlike soldiers or terrorists who must be trained. Yet every aveirah is a subdivision of avodah zarah, as the Ba'al Shem Tov says.

title.en: The sotah and the spirit of folly

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that one sins only when a spirit of folly enters him, learned from the sotah, and builds the kal vachomer: one ready to die for avodah zarah should surely bear a small discomfort to avoid any aveirah, which is the same avodah zarah in disguise.

title.en: Folly, forgetting and the hidden love

summary.en: Starting chapter 25, the Rav distinguishes two settings of sin: faulty reasoning (shtus) and simply not thinking (shikchah). The remedy is to remember and arouse the hidden love, since a person who sins forgets his bond with Hashem, like the sotah who forgets her bond with her husband.

title.en: The Avnei Nezer on the kohenes

summary.en: The Rav brings the case of a kohenes who remarried on the word of one witness and whose husband returned. The Avnei Nezer explains that a bond like chassan and kallah exists between every Jew and Hashem, felt more strongly by Shevet Levi, so she should have sensed her husband was alive.

title.en: Love that includes fear, a G-dly instinct

summary.en: On 'in your mouth and in your heart', the Rav explains that the hidden love includes fear, like a mother holding her baby tightly on the stairs, and works as a G-dly instinct, like an animal giving itself for its offspring. So a person can surely break a small desire; and he notes that love is the root of positive mitzvos and fear of negative ones.

title.en: The plea of later teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav takes up the argument that a small aveirah can be fixed with teshuvah, and brings the Gemara that one who says 'I will sin and repent' is not given the means to repent. He explains that this means no heavenly arousal is sent, but if the person pushes his way in, the teshuvah still helps.

title.en: No 'temporary' above time

summary.en: The Rav shows that even with avodah zarah a person could do teshuvah afterwards, yet every Jew gives his life rather than be cut off even temporarily. The reason is that above there is no time, so an aveirah is stamped into eternity, and the soul feels it would lose its eternity.

title.en: Fighting laziness in positive mitzvos

summary.en: The Rav applies the same reckoning to positive mitzvos, with the example of missing Mincha for a ball game. Laziness comes from the element of earth, the most passive element, and one must fight it with strength in Torah, tefillah and tzedakah, the three pillars.

title.en: Victory removes the concealment

summary.en: The Rav says overcoming the yetzer hara is near and possible for everyone, and after victory the concealment is lifted and one feels close to Hashem. He explains 'Hashem Echad': no place is empty of Hashem, and the darkness of this world is only a blanket covering Him.

title.en: Shovevim: piercing the dark curtain

summary.en: The Rav connects this to the Shovevim weeks, the darkest season, when the work is to pierce the dark curtain and find Hashem within it. Chanukah prepares for it; today the darkness has entered our homes, and in these weeks of reading about the exodus one should extricate one's own soul from Mitzrayim.
